_ SPRING. Mindful of disaster past, • And shrinking at the northern blast, The fleecy storm returning still, The morning hour and evening chill, Reluctant comes the timid Spring; Scarce a bee, with airy ring, Murmurs the blossomed boughs around, That clothe the garden's southern bound; Scarce a sickly, straggling flower, Decks the rough castle's rifted tower; Scarce the hardy•primrose peeps From the dark dell's entangled steeps; O'er the field of waving broom, Slowly shoots the golden bloom; And, bit by bit, the furze-clad dale Tinctures the transitory gale; While from the shrubbery's naked maze, Where the vegetable blaze Of Flora's brightest 'broidery shone, Every chequered charm is flown. ODE TO SLEEP. And therefore am I seeking to entwine , A coronal of poppies for my head, Or wreathe it with a wreath engarlanded By Letlae's slumberous waters. Oh! that mine Were some dim chamber turning to the north, , With latticed casement, bedded deep in leaves, That opening with sweet murmur might look forth On quiet fields from broad o'erhanging -eaves, And ever when the Spring her garland weaves, Were darkened with encroaching ivy-trail And jacTed vine leaves' shade; And all its pavement starred with blossoms pale Of jasmine, when the wind's least stir was made; _ Where the sunbeam were verdurous-cool, before It wound into that quiet nook, to paint ! With interspace of light dnd colour faint That tesselated floor. How pleasant were it there in dim recess, In some close-curtained haunt of quietness, To hear no tones of human pain or care, Our own or others', little heeding there ' If morn (~r noon or night Pursued their weary flight, - But musing what an easy thing it were To mix our opiates in a larger cup, And drink, and not perceive Sleep deepening lead his truer kinsman up, Like. undistinguished Night, darkening the skirts o Eve. —Archbishop Trench.

When are watches easily stolen? When they are off their guard. The Scotchnaan who tumbled off a bicycle says that in future he intends to "let wheel alone." We have but a short pilgrimage here ; we ought to keep 'together and cheer each other on the road. There is a difference in milkmaids; the milk made in the country is not the same as the milk made in the city. "Courtin'," says Artemus Ward, "is like strawberries and cream—wants to be ,did slow; then you git the flavour." A society journal informs us that "when a gentleman , and lady are walking up the street, the lady should walk inside the gentleman." An American farmer, speaking of the thinness of his hay crop, said, "The- grasshoppers have all got lame I trying to jump from one blade of grass to another. But you know, pa," said the farmer's daughter when he spoke to her about the adtiresses of his neighbour's son, "you know, pa, that ma wants me to marry a man of culture!" "So do I, my dear, so do I; and there's no better culture in the country than agriculture'!" Probably there is not one of us who has come to middle age who does not often have moods in which he would gladly lay down his own old self., and be literally born again—a new man, unfettered by past obligations, un- injured by past mistakes. We dream about what we would do, if we could begin anew; but dreaming is only dreaming, and wishes are not horses for any of us to ride. Such as we have made our own lives we must live them. A NEW YORK DAUGHTER.—The winter of 1783 was very severe, and the sufferings of the poor in New York City were unusually great. A family, numbering hus- band, wife, and daughter, were without fuel and food for some hours, and death by cold and hunger stared them in the face. The parents were infirm, and the daughter had supported them for some length of time, but now she could obtain no work. While she was sorrowing over their suffering condition she remembered that a dentist had advertised for sound fore teeth, offer- ing three guineas each for all he was allowed to extract. She immediately repaired to his office, made known the condition of her parents, and offered to dispose of her fore teeth on his terms. Instead of extracting her teeth the dentist gave her ten guineas, and sent her rejoicing home. Who can doubt that there were elements in that girl's character which, properly developed, would have distinguished her in any sphere? FILIAL PIETY: CAZOTTE'S DAUGRTER.—It is related of the distinguished Frenchman Cazotte, that he was im- prisoned with his daughter, and both awaited their trial. No proofs of the charge could be found against the daughter, Elizabeth, a very lovely and accomplished young woman, and she was ordered to be released. But the noble-hearted girl refused the offer of liberty, and determined to share imprisonment with her father. For some time the father was spared out •of respect to the fidelity of his daughter. But on the second of Septem- ber, 1792, Ile was summoned to meet death. He was led forth, and the axe waS already uplifted to sever his head from his body. At that moment, Elizabet 4 rushed through the crowd and threw herself upon hef father's neck, exclaiming," Strike, bartarians ! you shall net get at my father until you have pierced my heart'!" The hand's of the murderers dropped, and they stool power- less. " Pardon !" shouted one. " Pardon ! Pardon !" shouted a thousand voices. Elizabeth was allowed to lead her father forth to liberty and his home. THESE AoPorsrren SEASON.—Where is the cuckoo? Where is the nightingale? Where are the swallows? They are even now on their way towards us, ready to give their aid in preserving the balance of Nature. The cuckoo will be with us as soon as the great hairy .cater- pillars have begun to be troublesome—caterpillars which no bird. but the cuckoa can swallow. Not yet is the nightingale wanted, his food not being ready for him. But he is on his way, and long before spring has passed into summer his matchless song will be heard. Where are the swallows? Likewise on their way, and as soon] as the gnats, midges, and other small flying insects are beginning to swarm, the swallow will-be wady to ,eat them. The night-jar, toe, is preparing for its journeyto our shores. It performs during the night the same task -which is assigned to the swallows- by day; and its long- drawn jarring cry will soon tell us that it is helping the agriculturist by eating the moths, chafers, he., which, if allowed to increase unchecked, would seriously damage the crops. With what wondrous tare is the whole economy of Nature arranged, each creature making its appearance exabtly at its appointed season, and each of them being constituted so as to work in correspondence , with the sweep of the earth through its annual track of five hundred and seventy millions of miles, nothing being great or small in the eyes of the Creator I—Rev. J. G. Wood, in Smeday Magazine. CALCITLATION AMONG SAVAGES.—I don't knew how far the Damaras themselves can count; but the Chiquitos of America, a very low Indian tribe, couldn't count -be- yond one; for any larger sum than that, their simple language used terms of comparison alone—as many as one's eyes, as many as a crow's toes, as many as the fingers on one hand, and so forth up to six or seven. The Tasmanians could get as far as two; beNmnd that, they stopped short; their simple scheme of numeration was merely this—one, two, a great many- The Australian black-fellows in Queensland go a step further—they reckon thus: "one, two, two-one (3), two-two (4) ;" and after that, they say," more than four," meaning thereby an indefinite number. One South African tribe easily beats this rudimentary record, and knows how to count tin to ten. ,But eleven, or both hands and one over, it regards as the ne ;km ultra of human computation. When a British detachment once marched agamst it,the :scouts brought in word to the elders of the tribe that an immense army was coming to fight them*" an immense army eleven white soldiers !" On the other hand, some savages have really very advanced systems of numera- tion; for example, the Tong,ans, whose native numerals go up as far as 100,000. Even this degree of proficiency., however, did not quite satisfy the devouring mathe- matical passion of Labillardiere, who asked them what they called ten times that number, and so en until he had finally made them give him names for all the subsequent decimal stages up even to one thou- sand billions. The polite Tongans, anxious to oblige a benevolent and generous scientific gentle- man in so unimportant a matter, proceeded at once to supply,. him with words, which the unsuspecting ex- plorer immediately wrote down, and duly printed as mathematical terms in the accounts of his travels. But alas for the duplicity and the unscrupulousness of savages T.The supposed numerals in their higher ranges were really the rudest and naughtiest words in the Tongan language, with which, as missionaries subse- quently discovered, the evil-disposed Polynesians had successfully imposed on the bland and child-like inno- ,hence of a scientific stranger. Such are the dangers of leading questions addressed in an imperfectly wader- stood tongue to the' wicked minds of the children of , nature The children Of nature promptly respond in -the precise'spiritt, of an East End arab. The basis of all primi- tive habit arithmetic,ocounting lf may be safely asserted, lies in the primi- on one's fingers. Not only do all savages children and all so count at the present day ; not only do we all learn our first arithmetical lessons on that simple and natural portable abacus • but also all our most advanced numerical methods bear still upon their very face the evident marks of their evolution from the old mode of reckoning on the human hand. For the decimal system itself is a living result of the fact that every man (bar accidents) has ten fingers, and ten only. Nay, the very word "digits," by which we still express in the most abstract manner the symbols • of the numbers, points back at last to the tenimheld black fingers of the original savage.—Cornhill Magazine for KAY'S CONIPC•END, for Colds and Coughs. Woman (begging)—" Won't you help a poor woman Who has been left alone in the wide, wide world ?" Sailor who has been shipwrecked—" That's nuthin', mum. You'd hey sumthin, to complain about ef you'd bin like me, alone on a wide, wide sea." . _ _

Teaeirsr—" John, what are your boots made` of ?" Boy —" Of leather, sir." Teacher—" Where does the leather come from?" Boy—" From the hide of.the ox." Teacher —" What animal therefore supplies you with boots and I shoes, and gives you meat to eat ?" Boy—" My father." One of our brother journalists went into a barber's shop the other day to have his hair cut, and fell asleep during the operation. The barber, who awoke him I -when he had finished, said to him, "You are tired. I understand it. It's the same way with me when even- ing comes. Ah, this head work is something terrible !" A Ftsu STOEY.—One of the stories hi which a pe- culiar Christian name figures is of an accident that hap- pened when Preserved Fish, just twenty-One years old, had been made captain of a New Bedford whaling vessel. A revenue cutter bore down upon him and demanded the name of the brig. "The Flying Fish," shouted back the young commander. "What's the cargo ?" was the next question. "Pickled fish," was answered. "And who is captain ?" "Preserved Fish !" That Government officer couldn't stand this. He did not propose to be fooled with and made fun of by anybody in this way, and on board he climbed with his lieutenants, only to find that the whole truth and nothing but the truth had been told him.—Americart Angler. A farmer living in one of the interior counties of Cen- tral Mississippi shipped ten bales of cotton to a New Or-. leans merchant, and in due time received a letter ac- knowledging the receipt of the cotton and giving market quotations, &c. The letter was written by; a type-writing machine. When the farmer got it he was quite angry, and immediately wrote to the merchant that " He needn't think that because he lived in the pine woods that he had no education; that he was very grateful to his father, who had sent him to school, and had had him taught not only to read, but to read writing, so the next time he had occasion to communicate with him he Could write, and not go to theexpense of having his letter printed." CABBY EQUAL TO THE OccAstox.—Elderly Party: Hi, Cabby! Drive me to Barnes, and—ahem !--I hire you by the hour !—Cabby (testily) : Couldn't do it, sir. Just removed a smallpox patient from a private 'owe to , the 'orspitaL Goin' to the yard to get disinfected.—Elderly Party (blandly) : Don't trouble aboutthat, my good man; I'm just recovering from a very severe attack of. the Self- same dangerous complaint myself; so you will just suit me.—Cabby (fairly alarmed): Werry likely, old crumpet face; but you won't soot me. There's a hempty ham- bulance and a hempty 'earse a-follerin' hon. Pick yer chice o' them wehickels ; they'll take by the hour, day, or job, at a invalid's pace too, you bet. (Drives off at fire engine speed.)

AN EXPLORER'S TROUBLES ON THE UPPER For three weeks, Seago and I have laad a soul-siekening fight for the mastery with our entire caravan, and in the course of it we have had to brandish our revolvers like transpontine stage brigands, use our fists and our tongues like natives of Billingsgate, and hourly tear the passions to tatters, while our men have jeered at, threatened to murder us, and in a thousand ways to frighten us; and bring our plans to contemptible failure. Can you wonder now why I spoke of myself as a bruised reed? But, mark you, though bruised, I am not squashed. We have not indeed as yet got the upper hand; but we are making headway towards the victory .every day, and though we peel our knuckles in the ne- cessary .battle, we mean to win and to implant that respect for the white man which the natives have failed to acquire under a foolighly indulgent government on the Coast.—Joseph Thomson in" Good Words" for April. THE PITI,LOT AND THE TELEPHONE.—At one of our Northumbrian pits lately the telephone has been laid into the clerk's office. Other' fruits and vegetables have risen in pro- portion. It thus, be seen that ,present prices are 100 per cent. Mid' upwards higher than they were forty years ago: Can the rise in rents, wages. &c., be com- mensurate with the improvement of the above-named articles of farm produce? With the introduction of sanitary measures into our towns and villages, farmers were deprived of an extensive source of manure supply, and they had naturally to cast about for a substitute. This was offered to them in artificial manures, and in their ignorande of the properties of these stimulants,' they used them not wisely but tho' lavishly, to the detri- ment not only of their means, but to the injury of the crops, the soil, and the animals fed upen thecrops grown by them. liere, we believe, is the secret of the distress from which so many farmers have been suffering, but the lesson ought to be plain, although the recovery will occUpYsome time. Another reason for the depression may be found in the fact that ih their antagonism to trade unionism, farmers placed too much importance to the rise in the ,rates for labour; and have elected to allow their dand to fall .into a dirty state rather than employ necessary aid to ensurer clean cultivation, forgetting that weeds require more nutriment, being,grosafeeders, than do the crops .or the fain,. In most casei it has been sought to atone for this lack of cleanliness by heavier manuring of the soil. This is a mistake. A maw can but eat and assimilate one dinner at a time; so it is With the land and the crops, .and any excess 23 hurtful to both. Crean cultivation and moderate manuring will produce the best and soundest crops; dirty land and ex- cessive manures lead to poverty and disease.

Devonshire, biker Hall, for over 400 guineas, and is by 3rd Duke of Hillhurst, sold for 3,000 guineas. • ENSILAGE.—A SUGGESTION.—In filling my silo with vetches and rye I purpose adding brewer's grains at the rate of one bushel to every two c wt. of green stuff. This addition of grains will, I perceive, fill up the interstices of the silage so as to exclude the air more completely, will Sooner set up fermentation, and I hope will add to a more pleasant flavour to the silage. Brewer's grains can be purchased in the summer time cheaply, and as a pro- ducer of, milk and well-flavoured butter we have all I aniple experience. Is there anything to prevent it being I a success?—D. C.

• DEPRECIATION IN THE VALUE OF LANDED PROPERTY IN YORIESHIRE.—In 1879, on the death of the late Mr. W. Fewster, a gentleman well known in North Yorkshire, his small freehold residential estate, comprising residence (t*elve rooms), hunters' stabling, farm, ktd/1,37 acres of first-class arable and pasture land, situate close by Earl Carlisle's Yorkshire seat, was sold by auction for £12,500. The estate was then sold subject to the pay- ment of an annuity of £5O per annum- On the 24th ult. the estate wag again offered for sale at Malton:without the latter incumbrance. The highest offerlthat could be obtained was £7,000. The reserve put upon the estate was £9,000, AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' WAGES.—A bill to amend the law of bankruptcy, so far as relates to agricultural labourers' wages, has been brought into the House of Commons by Mr_ Stanhope, and is backed by Mr. Comp- ton Lawrance, Mr. Sclater-Booth, and Mr. Long. A me- morandum sgts forth that the Bankruptcy. Act, 1883, enacts, in sec. 40, that in the distribution of the property of a bankrupt there shall be paid in priority to all other debtsrinter alia, all wages of any labourer or workman, not exceeding £5O, whether payable for time or piece- work, in respect of Services rendered to the bankrupt during four months before the date of the receiving order. The bill proposes to amend this section by meet- ing a case which arises among yearly labourers. It is a common case in many counties that some labourers are hired by the year, and a part of their wages become due and payable only in a lump sum at the end of Ole year of service; the result is that in case of the bankruptcy of the employer during the year of servicelthe labourer gets po.part of the lump sum, or if it occurs. after the completion of the year of service, and the sum is :not paid, the labourer can only obtain priority in respect' of one-third part of it. ,_ _ _

IN SILAGE.—" Alsike " asks the cause of mil- dew down the sides of his silo, and what are the ibest means of preventing it? "My silo was filled last year with a second crop of clever, which was put in very dry. It came out very .much like very good clover hay. There was, however, a considerable loss around the sides by mildew, which lam anxious to avoid %is year. Would the walls, having been built only two months before;the silo was filled, cause thd mildew? The walls are of strong brickwork, lined with Portland cement. My pres- sure is Reynolds' Patent; and the clover was covered with planks, not quite closely fitted together, as I was told to allow a small distance between for the escape of the air on the pressure being exerted. The ensilage ex- periments at Woburn seem to have been a complete stic- cess, and I should very much like to know how the:loss by mildew was obviated ?" The floating spores of one or another form of fungus, producing mildew, seeth to be everywhere and when they alight on surfaces of any animal or vegetable matter not absolutely dry or frozen, they will grow and develop in some form of mildew. The only remedy is to exclude air, and that is to some extent done by pressure. If your silage were packed as closely against the wall of the silo as it is against itself in the midst of the silo, there *ould in all probability be no more mildew in those portions than the others. But you cannot manage this, and therefore there will always be some liability to mildew on the outside. Pack-closely, and press specially where the liability is greatest. BREEDS AND BREEDING.—Mr. Primrose M'Connell, con- tinuing his dairy lectures, writes:—lf we compare the capabilities of cows of olden time, where we can find them recorded, with those of to-day, as regards the quantity and quality of the milk, we are struck with the great improvement that has taken place, and how much better our animals are than those of our forefathers. This improvement is the result ofibreeding ; "artificially selecting" the best animals only to propagate their species, fostering their milk-yielding power by all ex- ternal means, and" weeding- out the bad specimens. Not only, however, is there a great difference between ancient (as in the wild white cattle) and m4dern cows, but in any existing herd no two animals will be found equally good, though all are placed under exactly the same cir- cumstances. It is an undisputed fact that the same pasture and food will keep a good cow just as well as an inferior One, while the 'latter may be kept at a loss. As an example we may take the case of two cows yielding respectively 400 and 600 gallons of milk per annum. At market price ;their food may. be taken at £l6, and the milk-at 81. per gallon. The inferior animal will give a loss of £2 13s. 4d., and the good one a profit of £4. This difference is a constitutional one in most cases, bred in the animals. The result of long practical experience teaches us that the only way to improve these matters and make all our cows yield 600 gallons or over, of 'good quality, is first of all to use a bull from a good milking family, and to rear the calves from good milkers only. The great rule in breeding is that "like produces like," and any charac- teristic of a breed becomes more and more defined and ,conspicuous according to its being repeated and adhered to generation after generation. In some of our native breeds the milking function has been altogether lost sight of, and the animals have been developed for beef "only; but in others—some seven or eight kinds—the quantity and quality of the milk have been the chief concern. It has-been alreadyspointed out that difference of .quality may be due to a difference in the micro- scopical structure of the milk, +which in its turn may be the result of a characteristic peculiarity of the breed, as we see in the case of the Jersey and Ayrshire. The im- mediate parents have always ibe niOst influence on their progeny, but sometimes there may be a "dormant in- fluence" at work, and a bad point may come out in the offspring of well-bred parents. This phase of matters —known as "atavism or "harking back "—is due to heredity, and points back to the ancient ancestors in many cases. Again, sometimes one male may have more influence on the offspring than ,others—that is, the progeny of other bulls may take after one special sire. This influence, which we call " pnepotency," and which may be as much mental as physical, is of great impor- tance, and in practice it is advisable, on accolint of it, to use-a first-claas sire in breeding from a heifer. Messrs. J., H. 'Truman and Son, Bushnell, 111., have sold the Shire stallion Honest Heart to Mr. J. L. Griffith, of Bushnell, 111., for £4OO.

THE AGRICULTURAL PROBLEM. • [FROM A COURESPONDENT.I Were the question asked, Why is it that farming does not pay in the present day? it would, no doubt, receive various replies from agriculturists, having reference to the nature of their farms—,arable, pasture, or mixed. From the first we should have the reply that it was owing to foreign competition, producing low prices for British produce, and a sequence of wet seasons; from the second and third the replies would be—high rents , and advanced rates and taxes; higher wages for labour, and bad markets. . Although each and all of these have had their effect in reducing profits in farming, yet we venture to say that, even when combined, they have not been sufficient to produce the widespread distress that has prevailed in agriculture during the past few years. This more espe- cially applies to farms where the breeding, rearing, and fatting of live stocks prevail, and also to dairy farms. In a lesser degree it is applicable to purely arable farms. There is another reason that has probably been more potent of evel than any of the above—namely, the costly system of manuring the land that has sprung up of late years, resulting from the absence of reliable information on the part of the great body of farmers in relation to what is now known as scientific farming, whereby they have been led into excessive expenditure, without any resultant adequate return for such outlay. Not alone is it true as to this premise, but, as in all excesses, not only have the crops failed to give a profitable return, but the products grown thereby have suffered in quantity, quality, and soundness. If we go back thirty to forty years, we find that prior to the epoch of artificials, our• farmers sustained the fertility of their soils by such fen, tilisers as farmyard manures, bones, lime, soot, and night soils, and that nothing was then heard as to the fertility , of the soil being exhausted. Under this system, both ' soils and crops were healthier and also more productive than now. At the present day, we grow a heavier yield of roots, such as turnips, mangolds, and potatoes, but the percentage to be deducted for rotten tubers reduce them probably below the old level, and there can be no doubt but that the crops grown under the old system had greater and healthier nutrition for live stocks. Further, if we go back to the time indicated, 'we find that all the products of the farm, gran excepted, were lower in price than they are at the present day. Flesh meat in this district then sold at from 3d. to 7d. per lb.; butter, Bd. to 9d. per lb.; potatoes, ltd. to 2d. per Stone; eggs, froin 20 to 30 for _ is.; new milk, 2d. per quart; skim milk, id. per quart; ,apples, 2d. to 3d. per measure; pears, 3d. to 4d. div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. TM MALAY FOWL
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. TM MALAY FOWL

The breed of domestic poultry mast nearly resembling the Gallus Bankiva, which is thought to be the ancestor of all our .domestic breeds of poultry, is the Malay. It is also very similar to the indigeneus fowl of India, which it resembles in many characteristics. It is. very many years since it was first imported into England, and there is mention made of it in books thirty and forty years old as a breed then well known. It, of course, derives its name from the Malay peninsula, .whence it was first brought over to*England. It has never reached the position Of a favourite fowl, but there have always been a nutnber of breeders who have con- sistently stood by it. The reasons forthis want of popu- larity are not far to seek. The appearance of the bird is so much against it, and its pugilistic proclivities have made it .a bird very difficult to, keep in lame numbers. It is also a poor layer, and this lack has not been made .up by- any especial suitability for table purposes. It isl very true that the flesh is good in flavour, though a little strong, and wonderfully abundant, considering the ap- pearance of the fowl, but the heavy yellow shanks are ' not a recommendation upon the poulterers' stall?. These considerations have all combined to keep the breed in the background, and we question whether, under any circumstances, it is likely to beeonie a really popular variety. But the breed has its admirable points, and it is a satisfaction to know that it has beemmain- tained pure through all these years. The description given below from an old book on poultry will, in all the. essential points,, stand for the Malay of to-day, and. it, has undergone fewer modifications, perhaps, than any other of our breeds of fowls, the Dorking alone ex- cepted. , , The utilitarian value of the' Malay is in its admirable crossing qualities. Its flesh is a little high in' flavour for an uneducated taste, but when properly hung it makes a very fine dish. When crossed with some other suitable breed,the progeny, is a splendid table fowl. For this purpose there is nothing better than the dorking—say, dorking hens to• a malay cock. Size of body, qualityi and quantity of flesh are all secured, and the chickens are easily reared and hardy. Cockerels of this cross have often been killed weighing 181.bs. the couplef Almost as good a result can be obtained by crossing the' Malay with the Houdan the Crevecceur, or the La Fleche, the mild and delicate flesh of these breeds blend- ing well with the stronger meat of the Malay. The eggs. produced by this breed are very rich indeed, and have thick shells. The hens do not make good mothers, and on that account are not generally trusted with maternal duties, - though they make admirable sitters. The chickens should not be hatched MuCh before May, for they are slow in feathering, and if hatched too early ap- pear to feeil the cold very keenly. They bear confine- ment very well, and unless they did so it would be im- possible for anyone to keep them, as only tin ee or four will live peaceably together. The following description we cull from Mouhray's work on Poultry, puglished nearly 40 years ago : These birds are of gigantic proportions, and attain to a remarkable size; they stand 27 to- 28 inches high, and can readily pick food at a height of nearly three feet • from the ground. The form is remarkably long, and the body slopes down at a very sharp angle from the bottom of the neck to the commencement of the tail; the weight" of the cock is from 91bs. to nibs. (generally), although the prize bird at Birmingham Show in 1852 weighed 11i lbs. ; and in a letter At° the Royal Dublin'Agricultural Society, Mr. Rutherfo.'d states tlrat he had one unfatted that weighed 131bs. The hen averages in weight from 71bs. to 91bs., but the prize one at the above-named exhibition weighed 10-41bs. ; the bill is short, strong, and curved, of a yellow colour, the comb is of a peculiar form, singularly stunted and depressed, extending scarcely so long as the top ,of the head itself, but coining well forward on the forehead; it is sometimes described as a double comb, cut short off and flattened; but this conveys only a very poor idea of the correct form and appearance. It looks' in shape on the top as if it consisted of four or five small horse-beans enclosed beneath a bright red skin, very tightly stretched over it, se as distinctly to show the form of the beans; indeed, the comb is not unfrequently now described as a "pen or bean comb." Occasionally we have heard of Malays with small, single, upright combs, but we, should be inclined -to regard any birds as not true- I bred that did not possess the form of comb we I have described above. The wattles are almost entirely wanting, but there is a quantity of loose red skin which surrounds the ,cheek as if to supply its place. The eyes are fine, large, and bold and piercing in their glance— usually red—with the iris of a bright yellow, but some- times the eyes are what is termed "pearled" round the 'edges with almost a white colour; the head is singularly neat and clean-shaped, formed, as it has been constantly described, like that of a "serpent," sleek, depressed on the top. and elongated; the neck is extraordinarily long, sometimes reaching ten inches, and owing to the feathers of the neck being very close set, and not being more abundant at the bottom (as is commonly the case in other fowls) than at the top, the neck appears almost % i entirely of a uniform thickness of aboutnches round; the throat for about an inch beneath the lower bill is en- tirely destitute of feathers. The general plumage is of a very bad and close texture, the colour being a rich brown or dark chestnut, darked much on the breast, back, and thighs; the wings long and projecting down- • wards to the ground, the coverts of a rich glossy metallic black, the quill feathers lighter—that is, about the same shade as the feathers on the breast, the under and hinder parts much resembling those of a trimmed Game epck ; the legs are of a light yellow or straw colour, with a pinky OT ruddy streak down the side; both the shanks and thighs are of a most• mon- strous length, sometimes falling but little short :of 12 inches! The bones of the legs are very stout and strong, and the skin is covered with large though not coarse, scales, the tail flowing and erect, but neither large nor long, with some few beautiful sickle feathers falling .gracefully ever, and tapering gently to points—generally of a black colour—with dark-blue-and-green metallic re- flections in it; the neck and rump hackles, of the variety above described, a beautiful deep, rich brown, the feathers being extremely- glossy and shining. The hen is, of course, much smaller than the male; the sante bill and comb, though the latter is smaller; no wattles, but a bright-red skinny face and cheek; the same " ser- pent ' head; the neck very little shorter than that of the cock, and carried in a similar erect and dignified manner'; the wings long and projecting downwards to the ground in a much greater degree than any other 'fowl; the legs of the same colour, and very nearly as long as those of the male; the tail feathers (said to be five in number on each side) very straight and carried erect, over-lapping one another like a fan, and project- ing one beyond the other so that the last or upper feather is the longest. The colours of a hen to match the cock described above would be, the wings and back a deep brown, the neck and rump hackles of a lighter or fed- dish brown, and the feathers of the breast and under and hinder parts of a still lighter shade; the tail feathers black or very dark brown. The breed commonly known some years since appears to have been a rich deep red, the back an orange-red, neck hackles deep ruddy- brown, somewhat of a lighter shade than the feathers of the rump hackles. This sub- variety we think the neatest and handsomest of all. There is a very beautiful sub-variety of white Malays, the plumage of which is "snowy-white," except the feathers of the hackles, which are strongly tinged with a lemon or light yellow colour. There are also some hens we have seen nearly black, streaked with brown and yellow, rather prettily; but we have nevqr seen a cock that would match them, and they have,been placed with red or brown cocks. The breed Many years ago was much More prized than it has been for some time; and we greatly fear that it is fast disappearing in this country, a matter to be regretted, we think, by all true poultry fanciers.

It is stated that the Ameer distressed.—The Commander-in-Chief, accompanied Qir H. Sandeman, and escorted almost entirely by the Belooch sirdars and their tribesmen, reached Hurnai tt„ Thursday. Sir F. Roberts is greatly pleased with the ti,`eflgth of the frontier, the loyal feeling and prosperity of „Zstribes, the peaceful state of the country, and the develop- -lest of its resources. Orders have tto`h nent to the Turkish commanders on the Turco-Greek kelltier ,to assume the aggressive on the first hostile move- on the part of the Greeks. ter IRENs. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT-

THE " C.D." ACTS.—The Contagious Diseases Acts Re- peal Bill passed through committee without amendment, and was read a third time amid some cheering. SUNDAY CLOSING BILL.—The adjourned debate on the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sun- day Bill was resumed.—Viscount CRANBORNE opposed Ow bill.—Sir J. PEASE explained that by the bill howes would be open in the country on Sunday from half -past twelve to half-past two; and from seven to nine, instead of from six to ten.—For the second reading there voted 101, against 41. IldisnannANEous.—Several bills were advanced a stage, including the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill, and the Intoxicating Liquor (Sale to Children's) Bill, which were read a second time. The House adjourned at one o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at four o'clock. ZEBEHR PASHA AND THE SOUDAN.—Lot d RIBBESDALE called attention to the detention of Zebehr Pasha at Gib- raltar, and to the effect of such detention upon the Soudan provinces, and moved "That the time has come when under certain conditions Zebahr presence in the Soudan might prove valuable in the interests of Egypt and the pacification of the Soudan provinces."—Lord DrxDONALD hoped that their lordships would give no support to the motion. The antecedents of Zebehr were as bad as bad could be.—Lord FITZGERALD pointed oat that, though Zebebr Pasha might have been guilty of rebellion against the Ehedival Govern• ment, he was not a rebel against England.—The Earl of ROSEBERY said as soon as the Government could do it with safety they would release him, but it was difficult to imagine on what grounds anyone could arrive at the conclusion that Zebehes presence in the Soudan at the present time might prove valuable in the interests of Egypt and the pacification of the Soudan provinces.—The motion was negatived with- out a division. • THE IRISH QurisTrox.—The Earl of COURTOWN presented a petition from the General Synod of the Church of Ireland against any measure endangering the legislative union be- tween Great Britain and Ireland.—The petition was read at the table. The Compenfation for Damages Bill and the Army (An- nual) Bill were read a second time. Their lordships adjourned at 6-10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE IRISH LAND ACT.—Mr. MORLEY, answering a ques- tion put on behalf of Mr. Sexton, said in round numbers down to the end of February last nearly £3,200,000 of the old rental of Ireland, with peor-law valuation of £2,400,000, had been dealt with under the Land Act, the judicial rents being £2,600,000. Nearly three millions of three were dealt with by the Land Commission, and the remainder by the county courts, asd the amount of rents fixed by the courts and by private agreement out of court was nearly the same. There were no means of knowing the exact agri- cultural rent of Ireland, but at the time of the passing of the Act it was estimated that 300,000 tenants could avail themselves of its provisions, and 250,000 might do so. By the end of February 208,000 applications had been disposed of, and over 4,000 were pending. STATE-AIDED EMIGRATION.—Mr. SETON-KARR asked whether the Government would take into consideration the ,formation of a permanent emigration department under the management of a responsible Minister, or would entertain and develops any scheme of State-aided or State-directed emigration ?—Mr. G. MORGAN replied that inquiries had been made as to how far the Colonies would be willing to receive State-aided emigrants in the current year. The rep- lies received were now under consideration, and would,with other papers, be presented on an early day. He added that arrangements were being made for the establishment of an emigrants' information bureau in connection with the Colonial Office. GREECE AND THE POWERS.—Mr. BRYCE, answering a question from Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, said that the Greek Government had not intimated their acceptance of the ad- vice of the Powers, and her Majesty's Government bad no information at their command which would enable them to say whether Greece will refrain from breaking the peace of Europe. THE SPOIL OF THE PALACE AT MANDALLY.—Sir U. KAY- SarrrLEwownt stated, in answer to Mr. Richard, that the Viceroy of India had reported that some time ago a quan- tity of precious stones and jewelry, a number of unbrellas, &c.. were found in the Palace at Mandalay. It had been decided to sell them, but a few of the jewels would be re- served for the Queen. A quantity of furniture was also found, and would be sold on the spot. REGISTRATION.—Mr. CHILDERS, in answer to Mr. T. Rogers and Sir Julian Goldsmid, said the Government did intend to introduce a bill during the present session dealing with the registration of Parliamentary and probably of municipal voters. He was unable as yet to say whether the bill would deal with any question of franchise or shortening the period necessary for a quali- fication to vote. THE PRESIDENT OF TRH LOCAL GOTERNMENT BOARD Mr. Stansfield, who was introduced by Mr. Leveson- Gower and Mr. Shaw, took the ~ath and his seat for Hali- fax on his re-election as President of the Local Government Board. The right boo, gentleman was received with Ministerial cheers. TRH Caorreas BILL.—The House was again in corn- committee on the Crofters Bill all the evening. Clause 6, relating to the fixing of rent, occupied several hours. A proposal by the Marquis of Stafford to extend it to lease- holders of not exceeding £3O was discussed for some time, and ultimately negatived by 230 to 121. At the instance of Dr. Macdonald and with the consent of the Lord-Advocate, seven years was accepted instead of 15 as the term for which the rent is to be fixed, and words were also inserted giving the Commission power to deal with arrears. A pro- posal made by Mr. Rogers that the rent should be in propor- tion to the current price of agricultural produce was dis- cussed at some length, but u.thnately withdrawn. Clause 11 was added to the Bill, and the committee adjourned until next day at 2 o'clock. The Bankruptcy Office Accommodation Act Amendment Bill was read a second time. The Prison Superannuation Bill was read a third time. SALE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS (DURHAM) BILL.—OR the motion that the Bill be read a third time, Mr. Tolima- sox moved that it be recommitted for the consideration of amendments which absent members had no. opportunity of moving in committee. (" Oh.")—After remarks from one or two members, the amendment was withdrawn, and the Bill was road a third time amid cheers. On the motion of Sir L. Playfair, leave was given :to intredma a Bill to amend the Medical Act, 1858. The House adjourned at 3 40. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. Misceeeeereous.—The report of amendments to the Lunacy Act Amendment Bill was read, and the Idiots Bill went through Committee.--The Marriage (Hours of Solemnisation) Bill was read a second time, on the motion of Lord MONS Beserron.--The Compensation for Damages Bill went through Committee.----Earl BEAUCHAMP gave notice that on the second reading of the bill for legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister, the Duke of Argyll would move its rejection. The House adjourned at 6-10. HOUSE OF COMMQNS.—TITESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. IRISH LOANS.—In reply to Mr. Albert Grey, Mr. FOWLER said that the loans guaranteed by the Government for Irish purposes since 1840 consisted of £12,267,000 for the pur- poses connected with the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and charged on the Irish Fund. Of this £4,673,180 had been already paid. Nothing bad been remitted on account of this loan. The loans directly advanced for Irish purposes between 1840 and 1885 amounted to £33 668.127; of this £17,693,820 had been repaid, and £9142000 re- mitted, leaving £6,834,305 outstanding. The loans due to the famine of 1846.9 amounted to £8,166 000, of which £7,000,000 had been remitted £1,267,300 had been ad- vanced in respect of a subsequent period of distress in 1879.81. Of this £19069 had been remitted, so that only £2,091,627 had been remitted in respect of loans other than connected with periods of distress. The loans to owners of land between 1840 and 1885 amounted to £7,591,600, of which £1,207,000 had been remitted, and £2.932 was out- standing. The losses to occupiers were £1,879,943, of which nothing had been remitted, and of which £847,410 was now outstanding. GENERAL ITEMS.—In reply to Sir C. Forster, Sir LYON PLAYFAIR said that the managers of public elementary schools had no right to refuse any child admission to a school if there was rocsm.--Answering Mr. Serjt. Simon, Mr. FOWLER said that the Prime Minister had requested him to say that in the present state of public business he could hold out no hope for giving facilities for proceeding with the Oaths Bill. THE SCOTCH CROFTERS' Bare—The House then resumed the consideration of the Crofters' (Scotland No 2) Bill in Committee.—An amendment moved by Dr. MACDONALD was agreed to, empowering the Commissioners to draw up a scheme regulating the use by crofters of seaweed, peat bog, and heather, or of the grass for thatching purposes, the charges for these being incleded in the rent.—Clause 12 as amended was then agreed to.---Clause 13 was next con- sidered. It defines what may be deemed available pasture, or grazed land, under the bill, and limits the power of the Commissioners to assign land for the enlargement of crofters' holdings by reserving gardens, parks, plantations, &c., and by restricting the enlargement to within an annual value of £ls.—Mr. CHAPLIN moved the omission of deer forests and sporting lands from those lands exempted by the clause from availability for the enlargement of crofters' holdings. He was speaking, when at ten minutes to seven o'clock, the debate stood adjourned. Mr. Latham took the oath aud his seat for the Crewe Division of Cheshire. THE DEATH OF MR FORSTER. At five minutes to seven Mr. GLADETONE, wee) rose amid subdued cheers from all parts of the House, asked for indul- gence while he expressed what he believed to be the general feeling of the House. He referred to the deep concern and regret which it felt at the loss sustained by the death of one of its most distinguished members, Mr. W. E. Forster, who undoubtedly obtained a high position by the success with which 19 years ago he had carried through that House the
NEWTON COMMISSIONERS AND THEIR, TOLLS.

At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, a case was argued before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, in _which the Newton-in-Alakerfield Improvement Commissioners sued a man named John Ogden, who had refused to pay toll to the plaintiff Commis- sioners under circumstances explained by their law clerk, Mr. Worsley, of the firm of Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, Warrington.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, was for the defence.—Mr. Worsley in- formed the judge that the case was precisely similar to one heard before his Honour some two years ago. In the case referred to Mr. Nash—whose sad death every one, no one more than himself, must deeply deplore—appeared for the Commissioners, and the whole question was, he thought, thoroughly and with very great fairness gone into. Seeing that the Commissioners had by their Act power of distraint, he could not too much regret that his - Honour should be troubled a second time with the matter. The title of the Commissioners commenced with a Royal grant Of King Edward the First, in which he granted to John de Langton, the then lord of the Manor of Newton and baron of the barony of New- ton, the right of toll and to hold fairs and markets in his barony, and from that time to the present fairs and markets had been held under that grant. In 1855 the New- ton Improvement Commissioners were incor- porated for the improvement of the town, and they obtained a private Act of Parliament, which Act gave them power to provide a market, and gave also the rents and tolls which they were authorised to charge. Amongst the tolls was specified the sum of ninepence for every horse cart load., which was the toll in this case demanded. After their in- corporation, the Counmissioners obtained an inden- ture of lease from the trustees of the Legh estates, Mr. Legh, of Lyme, being the descendant of John de Langton, by which indenture the trustees de- mised to the Commissioners a plot of land for a market place, and also all the fairs and markets to be held within the borough or township of NeY ton. . Subsequently a market was erected. On the 23rd and 30th days of January the defendant in this case was selling goods within the market, and was applied to for the toll of ninepence, which he re- fused to pay. The collector, instead of doing as he (Mr. Worsley) wished he had done, and seizing an article that defendant was selling' brought the mat- ter before the Commissioners, who instituted the proceedings. The Commissioners also claimed the sum of £5, which he should be prepared to reduce on the discretion of the court, for the disturbance of their market. He believed that the contention for the defence would be that the defendant was li- censed, which was the same contention last year.— His honour: Ido not think that can be contended now; is that Mr. Brown's defence? You do not contend that the license frees the man.—Mr. Browne intimated that he was prepared to make such contention.—His Honour said that lie had decided that once and for all. An excise *license merely gave him a legal right to sell anywhere in the kingdom, but did not allow him to sell in any particular franchise. His license was the same as one to sell tobacco or snuff.—Mr. Worsley: A man may have a license to shoot game, pheasants; but he has not a license to shoot them on my preserves. —His honour: It is just the same.—After some ' further conversation, his Honour gave judgment for plaintiffs for the recovery of the toll, granting costs on the higher scale, but making no order as to damages.

Although it was the fate of litia etlllenlte to differ from kirn On more *am sae important subject, which ised eisslst4bi totireosuct bean the Governmeat in 1880, there had sever beta the 'mallet% question as to the integrity of motive and leftimas of aim that had governed his public career. Although be had ceased to be a member of the Society of Friends, he cherished throughout his life that hearty love oil freedom which had always been a marked charecteristic of that society. (Hear, hear.) He never deviated how the straight path he had marked out for himself; he was a man of unflinching courage, and though a lover of peace he was profoundly attached to the greatness and welfare of the country. Whether they considered his ability or his moral aims, they could form no better wish for the country or the House than that the country might continue to produce such men, and that many might be elected to sit on the benches of the British House of Commons. (Cheers.) Sir M. Hicks-Buicx, who was cheered on rising, said after the eloquent tribute of the Prime Minister to the dic- tinguished member the House had so lately lost, he need only say be was confident that every member on that (the Opposition) aide of the House cordially sympathised with every word the right hon. gentleman had uttered, and felt they had lost in the late Mr. Forster a man of high courage, great ability, and sincere devotion to the interests of the country. (Cheers.) • The sitting was then suspended. A COUNT OUT.—At the evening sitting at nine o'clock, Duckbain had on the paper a notice to call attention to the unsatisfactory working of toe Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act of 1867, and to move a resolution that in order to stamp out pleuro-pneumonia, in the general in- terests of the nation it was necessary that the permissive powers given by clause 21, sub-section 2, of that Act should be rendered compulsory, and that the Act should be amended in order that the delegation of powers to the local authorities by the Privy Council might be so regulated as to pro- mote a greater uniformity in the orders for the movement of animals. Before, however, the hon. member had risen to address the House, attention was called to the fact that there was not a quorum, and the House was counted out at 0-5.

- HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after twelve o'clock. CHURCH PATRONAGE BILL.—A. new writ having been issued for Ipswich, Mr. LEeneatt moved the second reading of the Church Patronage Bill, which seeks to prohibit the marketing of advowsons, and contains clauses prohibiting the sale of next presentations, and also prohibiting resigna- tion bonds. The bill provides that all sales of adowsoas shall be void unless they are made te persons possessing or acquiring a property in the parish to which the benefice be- longs or the parish adjoining of the net annual value of the benefice itself. The maximum price is fixed at five years' value of the advowson.—Mr. RAIKES said the bill I in many of its provisioes appeared to be a desirable I measure, but he thought it might be amended.—Mr. RYLANDS nrged upon Churchmen and Dissenters that, in I view of the great change which he believed would come, it was their duty so to promote the reform of the Church in the meantime that when the change did come there should ' be less friction and less division of opinion.—Mr. HUBBARD pointed out the desirability of amending certain portions of the bill in Committee.—Mr. CHILDERS, speaking for him- self alone, thought the sale of advowsons and of next I presentations formed merely a small part of the great ques- tion of Churla reform in respect of temporalities with which sooner or later Parliament would have to deal. Mr. E. STANHOPE said there was now a general consensus of opinion that the law with I regard to Church patronage ought to be amended as soon as possible. He hoped the House would read the bill a second time, but that it would not be carried forward to committee until they saw the measure which the Archbishop of Canterbury was about to introtluce in the House of Lords. —Mr. A. GREY desired to see machinery provided to secure that the interests of parishioners should be properly re. spected.—Mr. F. S. POWELL remarked that they could not hope to get rid of the evils of patronage all at once, but it would be something to get rid of a portion of them. He held that the question of who nominated was a compara- tively small one, the real point being the fitness of the clergyman when appointed.—Mr. ILLINGWORTH could see no difference in principle and nefariousness between the sale of next presentations and the sale of advowsone, and he thought there was no radical remedy without disestab- lishment. Mr. CARVELL WILLIAMS also thought the difficulties complained of would never be overcome till the church was disestablished.—The ,bill was then read a second time. WATERWORKS Prue—Mr. G. BALFOUR moved the second reading of the Waterworks Rating Bill, and Mr. ADDISON moved its rejection.—Mr. STANSFELD suggested that further discussion of the measure should be deferred, and a motion for the adjournment of the debate was agreed to. Mr. BROADHURST announced that a Government bill with regard to the amendment of the Coll Mines Act was being prepared. and would be introduced immediately after Easter. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. .

The Lord6;ncellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Tbe Poor Relief klreland) Bill wa's brought from the Commons and read a first time. The Lunacy (Vacating of Seats) Bill and the Prison Officers' Superannuation Bill were read a second time. The Com- pensation for Damages Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to five o'clock.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

• An ordivery meeting of this Colin, 11 *as bald in tha Connell Chaser. 'Pawn Hall, on Tuasday evening. Thwe were present the Mayor (Al•terman Harrison), Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Webster, Crostleld ; Councillors Brown, Jolley, Dixon, Wright, Francomb, Ashton. W. Pierpoint, Mackie, Sutton, Fleming, Tinkley, Marsh, Greenall, Green- ing, Roberts, Hutchinson, Litton, Dakin, Bolton, J. Pier- point, Taylor ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Paterson (gas manager), and Chorley (borough treasurer.)

The estimated population of the borough is 46,000, and the estimated number of school.going children 7,700. : being one-sixth of the entire popolatien, and there are noel in ectual attendance at both public and private achoole 7,710, which is rather more than one its six.—Signed, on behalf of the committee, S. M. WESTER, Chairman. Alderman WEBSTER in moving the adoption of the min- utes and the report recapitulated the chief points set forth in the latter, and also remarked that the committee had al- ways felt that if the Town Council had more power with regard to education than they now have it would be a great advantage to the borough. They could not see why the School Attendance Committee of a Town Couticil should not have the same powers as a School Board. (Hear, hear.) If they bad these powers he thought they would use them quite as efficiently as a School Board. He thought also that an industrial school would be an advantage to Warrington, but with their present powers there was no chance of erect- ing one. With regard to half-timers, he considered thy were an unsatisfactory element. The cotemittee had thought they might safely be abolished by the time for com- pulsory attendance being diminished. They thought that up to fourteen years of age was a long time for working people to be compelled to send their children to school. (Hear, bear). Councillor DIXON seconded the motion. Alderman CROSFIELD said he was strongly of the same Opinion as Alderman Webster, and he thought it was a mon- strous shame that the School Attendance Committee of a Town Council should not have the same power as a School Board. (Hear hear.) That was the one great blot on poor Mr. Forster's bill, and he (Alderman Crosfield) knew at the time that Mr. John Bright strongly advised Mr. Foreter to give Town Councils the same power as a School Board, but he would not agree to do it. It was a great evil in a town like Warrington ; when the School Attendance Committee had so little power the consequence was, he believed, that they had 800 ragged children running about the streets of Warrington. In spite of all the splendid school accommo- dation they had, there were these children growing up in that state of ignorance. There were no means of reaching them, and he thought it would be a very good thing if that Town Council were to petition the Secretary of State for the Education Department, put these facts before him, and ask him to have an improvement made in the Education Act. (Hear, hear). Alderman BURGESS might say that he did not at all agree with the view Alderman Webster had been enunciating with reference to half-timers and it did appear to him (Alder- man Burgess) that the "drift ef Alderman Webster's argu- ment would require that there should be a special standard for each particular child, and that the standard should be adapted to the capacity of the child, and that would bring about a state of confusion which would be hardly tolerated. If the Act of Parliament was as bad as had been described, by all means petition Parliament for its improvement, but for his part be did not care how soon the t chool Attendancel Committee wis an abolished institution. He would infi- nitely prefer to see a School Board doing this work properly in Warrington. (" Question.") If an Act of Parliament had bad the attention of men of very great capacity—men like Mr. Forster., who was just dead, and all the best men in the House of Commons at that time, it was rather too much forthem to set up and criticise so very minutely and closely that Act of Parliament. Alderman CROSFIELD : It is 15 years old. Alderman BURGESS : Yes, and very good work it has done in the fifteen years and is doing yet, and it is doing its work better in towns where they lave School Boards than where they have not. Councillor MACKIE thought it was probable that the committee had not yet fathomed the depths of the powers given to them by the Act of Parliament, because be be- lieved they were far greater than anything that had been put in execution in this town. He remarked that a state- ment bad gone forth that there was not sufficient accom- modation for scholars in the town, and that unless they got one or ,two more schools they would require a School Board.
Alderman WEnsTEn; There is no official information to :at effect.

div.head: PROTEST.
div.p: A PROTEST.

The MAYOR said he had a communication in the shape of a memorial to which he particularly wished to draw the at- tention of Mr. Alderman Burgess because, perhaps, be would be more interested in it than some gentlemen there, The Mayor then read a memorial from ratepayers resident in the South-east and Yorth-east wards petitioning agAinst the construction of a urinal at the corner of Scotland-road in Buttermarket-street. The memorialists pointed out that the urinal would be an inconvenience to traffic; that similar places erected in other parts of the town became the loung- ing places of idelers and corner men; and that in fact the urinalwould be an intolerable nuisance, and would prove in- jurious to the inhabitants of the neighbourhood, ruinous to trade, and would cause a considerable depreciation of the I value of property in that locality. The memorial was I signed by a considerable number of persons, most of whom live or have their business premises in the neighbourhood referred to.

Alderman BURGESS said tbeY would not require him to anything about that memorial. In the first place it did not appear on the proceedings of that Council, and secondly it was out of its place there. The MAYOR: It is not out of its place. Alderman BURGESS : Permit me ; I would say that the urinal is now erected, and in action by the order not of my- self but of this Council.
The MAYOR: It is of course out of order to make a speech on the memorial.
Alderman BURGESS : I say this in consfquenee. of your appeal to me; it is the act of this Council and not of myself that that urinal is there.
The Mayor: All I intended was to draw your attention to

Alderman BURGESS: And all I intend is that the saddle should be on the right horse. (Laughter.) Councillor Macatia said he had been informed that the memorial had been supplied to the committee, and that those who presentad it did not meet even with the simple recognition that they had sent in any document as in other cases. He did not think that was creditable to the polite state the Warrington Town Council had long since reached. Alderman BURGESS: I wish you would give proof of any- thing you may have got to state. Councillor MACISIB : lhat is what I am asking for if you will allow me. .
..... ........ __. The Tows CLERK here pointed out that it was altogether out of order to enter into a discussion on that matter. The discussion on the subject then closed. WATCH COMMITTEE.

Hitchmough be accepted and that a gratuity of £2O be voted to him, he having resigned after eight years' service owing to continued ill-health. Recom- mendation that the tender of Mr. Matthew Chorley for the colouring and whitewashing at the bridewell at £lO be accepted. On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman WED. div.head: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING _COMMITTEE.
div.p: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING _COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended the following plans for ap- proval, viz. :—Four houses in Arply-street, for Mr. E. Fen- ton ; alterations at No. 1, Lloyd-street, for Mr. Joseph Dole- SOD ; eight cettaees in Chorley-street, for Mr. J. E. Wright; alterations to premises in Church-street, for Mrs. Jackson; ' alterations to premises in Gelborne-street, for Mr. Edward Connor; twelve cottages in'York-street, off Knuteford-road, for Mr. E. Jameson ; twelve houses in Orford-lane, for Mr. J. Appleton; alterations to premises in Buttermarket-street, for Mr. James Ross.—Recommendation, that the following estimate of expenditure by this Committee, for the half-year ended 29th September, 1886, be approved :—Street lighting, £l3OO purchase of land for street improvements, £300; sundries, £10; total, £l6lO. The MAyon moved and Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of these minutes. Councillor Dixon* remarked that there was £l3OO put down for the lighting of the borough for the next six months. When the gas works were purchased he believed it was Councillor -Sutton who told them that the profits of the gas works would he so great that the cost of the lighting of the borough would he very much reduced. Unfortunately, this last four or five years the cost of the lighting had increased. He was exceedingly sorry they had not true prophets about them. (Laughter.) . The MAYOR thought the increase in the cost of lighting was not exclusively confined to the borough. He thought all of them found from experience that their gas bills did not diminish as time went on. The minutes were then adopted. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—LONGFORD WOMB. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained the following :—Recommendation that the following estimate of ' expenditure by this Committee for the half-year ending 29th September, 1886, be accepted :—Nightsoil department, £2OBl 7s; tcavenging department, £1466 1s; nigh:soil depot department, £Bl2 ; hospital department, £430; total, .£4790 ss.—Resolution that a license be granted to Messrs. Lawrenson and Miller to slaughter cattle at premises in Ash- ton's Yard, Wilderspeol Causeway. Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes, and said he might just mention to the Council the fact that the machinery at lAngford was now in a state of completion. The day previous it was put in motion and is working as smoothly and satisfactorily as they could desire. As soon as the northern depot was finished, and he thought it would yet take about a month—he should ask the Council to be good enough to favour the Sanitary Committee with an inspection of their property and works at Longford,aud judge for themselves as to the results. Councillor Surrox seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to.
PAYING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes were as follows :—Recommen- dation, that the tender of Mr. William Bennett for 15 tons of Portland cement, at 40s per ton, be accepted. R.-com- mendation, that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Company. Limited, for carting setts and bar from Bank Quay wharf to Arpley-st..nynne-st., Jolley-st., and White- street, at 5d per ton, be accepted. ' Councillor WRIGHT moved, and Councillor ASHTON seconded, the adoption of these minutes, which was agreed to. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE'S REPORT : DISCUSSION

ON EDUCATION. The School Attendance Committee recommended that the following estimate of expenditure by this committee for the half-year ending 29th September, 1886, be approved :—ln- pectors' salaries, £9B lOs ; maintenance of boys at indus- trial schools, £4O ; sundries, £l5; total, £153 10s.—The average ettendance during the month of February at the public elementary schools was 6,889, and for the corres- ponding period last year, 6,691; increase 198. The committee also presented its report for the year ended 31st October, 1885, which was as follows :—The fol- lowing, which is the'eighth annual report of your commit- tee, bears very favourable comparison with the report for 1884, As usual, tabulated returns are furnished which contain valuable information. The average attendance at the public elementary schools in 1384 was 6,500; this year it has been 6,796, being an increase on the preceding year of 236. The increase last year was 199. At the end of September the number of children on the school registers was 8,881, including 181 half-timers. The numbers given by the school registers, however, are not to be relied on as correct; because in many instances a child's name appears on two or perhaps three registers of different schools, the code not requiring the name of a child who has left to be re- moved from the register until after six weeks' absence. The number of children attending private schools, includ- ing the Blue Coat School, the Grammar. School, and the Workhouse School, is 914, but it must be mentioned that nearly all the Workhouse children are in the schools at Padgate. In 1884 the number presented for examination was 7,084 : last year 7.424, showing an increase of 340 ; the increase of the preceding year was 68. There have been 331 cases, as against 381 last year, taken before the magistrates, in moat of which cesee fines were inflicted. Your committee anticipate now that the operation of the Education Act is becoming better understood, that this number will soon be greatly diminished. Four boys were sent to the tralaing ship " Clio " and two to the Industrial School, Liverpool. It is gratifying to learn that the con- duct of these boys is uniformly good, the reports from the " Clio " being particularly satisfactory. School fees have bsen allowed by the Board of Guardians for a large number of children, the amount being £142 17s sd. The fees allowed last year amounted to £ll9 2s 65. Trade is greatly depressed, and distress prevails to an abnormal extent, and in all probability there will be a still greater demand for fees during the current year. The expenses cf your committee, as taken from the borough treasurer's last published statement of accounts, 'as £340 16s Bd, which is only a little over £1 in excess of the expenses last year. The charge to the borough rate is a trifle over one half- penny in the X, without taking into account the sum received for fines, which amounted to £63 15s. Your isommittee have held 21 meetings during the year, and dealt with 430 cases, each of which was fully investigated. 'the school accommodation of the borough has been in- creased by St. Barnabas' school being built, which has pro- vided 500 seats, and your committee believe that in the course of a few weeks St. James' school, Latchford, which is now in course of erection, will be completed, and will provide additional room for upwards of 700 children. There is school acconamodation in the borough for 3,610 children over ani above the average attendance of the year, and your committee believe that this will amply satisfy the needs of the borough for some time to come, and effectu- ally prevent any cause for complaint on this ground. In one or two districts, however, the schools might be more conveniently placed, children having to wale some con- siderable distance to attend school, which is especially the Case in the Bewsey and Batte•sby-lane districts. With re- spect to the Battersby-lane district, however, your com• mittee have reason to believe that a committee has been ap- pointed for obtaining funds for the erection in this district of new elementary schools in connection with St. Elphin's parish. A site has been selected, and a sum of £1,600 promised by the Warrington Training College Committee towards the accomplishment of the object. The proposed school will provide accommodation for 200 boys and 300 girls and infants, and will, when erected, supply a long felt

mencing 28th March, 1888, at Is 3d in the pound, which is ' estimated to produce about £7,200. Resolution. that the ICouncil be recommendeti to authorize the nsaking of a 'sewers rate for the half-year commencing 2Gbi March, 1886, at 2d.: in the pound, which is estimated to produce about XO7O.

Alderman HOLMES, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said they had not quite provided sufficient moncy on the is 3d rate to cover the whole of the expenses which they bad anticipated, but they had always been informed by Akira-man Burgess and his brethren of the Sanitary Com- mittee that as coon as the manure works were in full opera- tion there would be a large amount of money saved. If they had not a sufficient amount the blame would rest en- tirelyon Alderman Burgess. (Laughter.) Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, which was agreed to.

div.head: PROPOSED RE-ARRANGEMENT OF POLLING DISTRICTS.
div.p: PROPOSED RE-ARRANGEMENT OF POLLING DISTRICTS.

Councillor W. PIERPOINT moved that the Council resolve itself into committee for the purpose of considering the desirability of dividing the wards into such number of polling districts as may be aeemed necessary and conveni- ent. He did not wish them, he said, to accept any scheme, although he had proposed one, and thought of placing it before the Council and asking them to confirm it. It would net interfere in any particular with the area of the wards, nor did it interfere with the present boundaries of the wards.

Councillor FRANCOMB seconded the proposal, and the Council agreed to resolve itself into committee. The Town Clerk then suggested that the reporters retire, as the Coun- cil was in committee; but, on the motion of Alderman Crostield, it was decided by a large majority that the repor- ters remain.

Councillor W. PIERPOINT then proposed "That a special committee be appointed to consider the present arrangement of the polling districts of the borough, and to report their recommendations as to any alteration of such districts at their earliect convenience, and that the follow- ing gentlemen form such committee :—Alderman Burgess, Councillors Sutton, Greening, Francomb, Wright, Jolley, W. Pierpoint, and Roberts" Councillor Srrrox seconded, and the motion after a short discussion was agreed to. The meeting then ended.

div.head: LIBERAL vicroßy AT BARROW.
div.p: LIBERAL vicroßy AT BARROW.

The polling to fill the vacancy at Barrow caused by ' the unseating of Mr. Duncan took place on Tuesday. Both sides used vehicles, the preponderance, however, being with the Conservatives. During the day showers fell at intervals. After five o'clock polling was carried on with considerable briskness, which added to the excitement, and there were a few lively encounters. The poll was declared as fohows
Mr. Caine (Liberal) Mr. Bruce (Conservative) Mr. Edmunds (Independent)
Majority

_ A crowd numbering several thousands gathered in front of the Town Hall. The figures were announced about a quarter past ten, and received with the most enthusiastic cheering. The Liberals justly claim this as a brilliant victory, inasmuch as they have had long odds against them in the face of what has been ex- plaincd as a Lobby intrigue, and the Catholic, Orange, Nationalist, Church, and licensed victualler's vote. Out of 6,063 on the register, 5,298 polled. At the last election, Mr. Duncan's majority over Mr Schneider was 346. Mr. Caine polled 551 votes more , than did Mr. Duncan, whilst the Conservatives have run down 438 votes, making an addition to the , Liberal majority, as compared with the last election, 'of 589 votes. Mr. Caine, in addressing the electors subsequently, said :—You have done your work nobly to-day. A FEVER SHIP. The British and African Royal mail steamer Congo (Capt. C. P:ichard), which has arrived from West Africa, landed four of the crew of the Welsh vessel Ethel Anne, which capsized and sank at Lagos. The Ethel Anne sailed from Gersten with coals for Natal, and after. wards went round to the West Coast to load palm oil for home. Whilst at Lagos many of the crew were stricken with fever, and two succumbed. Others had to be put in the hospital. As some of the vessel's timbers had become affected with rot, it was decided to hold a survey on her as she was lying outside the Lagos Roads. While waiting for this survey a tornado blew over the place, the Ethel Anne being thrown on her beam ends, and eventually capsized altogether. Through several men being in the hospital with the fever, there were only the captain, mate, and cook on board the Ethel Anne at the time. The men were picked up by a steamer and taken into Lagos. Ttie Ethel Anne herself filled and sank. KAY'S CoMPoUND, a demulcent anodyne expectorant, for Coughs aid Colds. bold by all Chemists, .9id, Is, Is lid, as 9d.--41drot.

The Hamer Spinning Mill, near Rochdale, belonging to Messrs. Shawcroft and Harrope, was al tkost totally destroyed by fire on Wednesday, the damage being estimated at £20,000. Several workpeople escaped from the building with difficulty, and were more or less injured. DEFECTIVE BAYONETS —Government viewers from En. field have been engaged at the Victoria Barracks, Windsor, in testing the bayonets of the let battalion of the Grenadier Guards. Out of 600 bayonets, 170 were c ,ndemuert as being soft, or as having small points, and 29 broke in the process of testing. TniSti REM, an aged Hindoo who has come from India for the purpose of bringing his grievarces before tLe Queen, was charged at Windsor, on Monday, with vagrancy. The prisoner, who promised to return to India, was re- manded, pending the arrangements being made ft,r his pas- sage home.

Davies (Con- servative) on the ground of corrupt pract;oes. The petitiost was dismissed, en Tuesday, by Mr. Justice Field, who con- sidered tbat there was no foundation whatever for the allegations made.

SEIZURE OF LAND BY CROFSERS —Last week the crofters on the Kintail estate declared that they were in such a low condition that they must take toe land which is lying waste into their own hemis to provide for themselves and families. Acing on this resolution, from 40 to 50 cottars tock posses- sion of a field and ploughed it, notwith,standing the remon- strances of Mr. M`lienzie's keepers. FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION.—A serious boiler explosion occurred on Monday in the flour mills of Messrs. A. and IL Tod, Commercial-street, Leith. The large building was destroyed, the roof being blown off and the walls thrown down. A scavenger working in the street was buried in the ruins and killed. Two brothers, aged 11 and five years, while playing in the street, were also killed Two fire- men at the mill were badly scalded. One of the boilers was burst by the force of the explosion, and the premises caught fire.
