GREAT FLOODS ON THE CONTINENT.—In consequence of the great accumulation of ice, which has become firmly wedged in between the banks, the waters of the Vistula have risen to such a height that both the town and harbour of Dantzlc have been in danger of being flooded. The dan- ger was diminished on S..turriav by the bursting of several dams and sluices and the loosening of the ice. The upper portion of the river is free from ice, bat the waters are still expected to rise several feet. Several places in the Valley of the Vist;ala have been terribly devastated by inundations. AN EMINENT COMPOSER.—Just now tile musical world of England is being taken by storm by Abbe Liszt, the eminent French composer, who is in London. On Monday Abb6 Liszt was present at a rehearsal of his oratorio "St. Eliza- beth "at St. James's Hall, London. Madame Albani, Mr. Santley, and Signor Foli were the principal vocalists, and Mr. islackeezie the conductor. The compooer took a per- sonal intPrest in the performance. He sat in the body of the ball, but at the end of each part he went up to the principal singers and shook them by the hand. He also intervened occasionally in order that Isis own expression might no given to the ins rgmentation. Since his arrival in London be has once privately given proof of his skill as an executant. On Wednesday the abbe Liezt paid a visit to the Queen at Windsor Castle.

FALL OF HOUSES: SEVERAL PER:IONS INJURED. -- llr Chatsworth-road, Lower Cla?ton, London, a number of s,mi-detached villas were approeching completion. On Saturday morning the front part of one house gave way, and the edifice collapsed, dragging the greater part of the ad- joining villa with it. A number of men were in the inte- rior, while others were on the scaffold. Five were buried beneath the ruins. Four of the men receivel severe cuts and bruises, while the fifth sustained a serious scalp wound and a fractured thigh. A plasterer, named Cook, who was knocked down and rendered senseless by the falling scaf- folding, had his left arm broken, besides having received an alarming wound across the hack of his head. Toe accident is attributed to subAdence of the land. MURDER OF A POLICEMAN.—On Sunday, P.C. Bentley was murdered at Leicester. during an affray with a drunken man named John Fox. Fox, a stranger in the town, went into a house and refused te leave, although the occupiers knew nothing about him. Subsequently they got him into the yard, and the police were sent for. Inspector Hawkins and P.C. Bentley went to apprehend him. On the way to the police station he became exceedingly violent, threw Bentley aside, and dealt him some very violent blows on the chest. Bentley reeled with the violence of the blows, which severely injured him internally, and fell helpless. A. terrible struggle ensued, but the prisoner was eventually overpowered and taken to the police station. Bentley was removed to the police station, and expired five minutes afterwards. A MASQLEIIAnER MURDERED.—A. rapid transition front comedy to tragedy is reported by the Paris co-respondent of the Lally 2Vears, who telegraphs on Sunday :—Thia morning the dead body of a ytiung man with painted face and dressed to resemble a Pierrot or Carnivalesque clown, was found in the ditch of the fortifications near the Roman. ville Gate, outside Belleville. A coloured silk handkerchief was knotted tightly around the neck of the deceased, who had been strangled and then thrown into the ditch. The victim is supposed to have been lured out to the fortifica- tions by some rival in the affectioNs of a woman, and there murdered in the manner described. A letter found in his pocket established his identity. He had been employed as a workman in a laundry at Lilas, and had participated on Saturday in the Carnival of the Mi-Careme, which is the great festival of the Parisian blanchisseuses. His name was SyPraha, and he was between 25 and 30 years of age._ . _ _

Tiill TRIAL OF TIM LONDON SOCIALISTS.—At the London Central Criminal Court, on Monday, the Recorder, address- ing the Grand Jury, referred to the charge of sedition against Burns, Champion, Hyndtnan, and Williams, and said the law permitted honest and bona fide criticism upon public affairs, hut it amounted to sedition where such language was used with a view to excite to acts of violence. In the pre- sent case it appeared that shops were plumiered and various acts of outrage committed, and the Grand Jury would have to consider whether the language which was used by the prisoners was .:attended with mala pes and with the illegal object of inciting the street mob to acts of ri,lence.—The Grand Jury returned a true bill against Messrs. Hynd- man, Champion, and Williams for uttering seditious language. The trial was begun on Tuesday; at the Old Bailey, London, before Mr. Justice Cave.—The Attorney-General said the defenants were charged with using seditious lanrzuaze and conspiracy. He referred to the facts already published, and thought it right to say that it was not suggested that the defendants incited the mob to particular acts of violence.—At the conclusion of the Attorney-General's opening, Mr. John White, repor- ter for The Times, gave evidence as to the characTer if the language used by the prisoners at a meeting at Hatton Wall, and also at the Trafalgar Square meeting. At Hatton Wall he heard Hvndman say he was a social revolutionist and feared no man. At Trafalgar Square Burns said the ' unemployed must have bread or they would have lead. He also heard the expression, that next time they would sack the bread shops in the West End. The witness gave other evidence as to the violent character of the speeches by the defendants.—Mr. Thompson examined the witness as to the accuracy of his report and evidence, but he adhered to his statement. He did not put in all the violent exclamations made at the meeting, because he thought it would probably cause great excitement, and possibly revolution, in London. On Wednesday the case for the prosecution was closed. The Judge, before calling on the defence, intimated that the defendants were not liable for disturbances that actually took place, as the prosecution did not sustain that allegation. Colonel Henderson and the Hon. Guy DawnaV were called as witnesses for the defence. The former said he did not anticipate any disturbance, unless in Trafalgar Square, and that was provided against. Mr. Dawnay said Burns protected him from the mob after his watch was stolen. Other witnesses followed, and the court adjourned till next day. Mr. Chamberlain was called as a witness for the defence. In answer to one of the defendants, he said he had never stated be was in favour of a revo'ution in the land tenure, though be was in favour of a reform. Mr. Childers was also called as a witness. Asked whether be had had any reports of rioting resulting from Socia'ist meetings, be declined to state what reports had reached the Home Office. He also said that no measure was now before i the Home Office for relieving the distress. The case was again adjourned. "FOREST TALES."—"MINNIGHEY" (both ithistra,ed by Sir John Gilbert. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY APRIL 10, 188 i.

- WARRINGTON and . t. Helens are alike Peculiar in being amongst the few larger towns that have not }et provided themselves with a School Board ; and it would seem that if they are left to their own initiative it !Jill be some time before they make a,move 11-1 this direction. There appears to be amorwst triany of the leading members of the corn- Illunity what we cannot but regard as an un- reasoning dread of the School Board system, a.ithougat the same time tire inconvenience acknowledged of the limited powers of 'chool Attendance Committees. The whole question of education was under discussion ,b4t the monthly meeting of the Warrington 'own Council, on Tuesday evening, and, as 111, ight be expected, there was considerable ,civersity in the expression of opinion. The cebate arose on the annual report of the School Attendance Committee for the borough, or perhaps we should say out of t,he speech which Alderman WEBSTER made moving its adoption. Of the report itself little need be said; it shows that Warrington, if not taking the lead in any respect, is keep- ing pace in the matter of providing school accommodation, notwithstanding much that has been foolishly said about having a School toard " forced on the borough" because of alleged failure in this respect. It is, indeed, stated that there is "school accommodation lithe borough lor 3,610 children over and attcve the average attendance of the year ;" la figures of this kind are somewhat mis- 4eading. What the law requires is not that the average attendance" shall be covered, csr something more than covered, but that there shall be a school place for every child "?f school age. The "average attendance" 's not recognised by. the Education Depart- -111, ent as a basis of operations in this conneo- „4°ll. What should be ascertained is the total 'llinber of children of school age, and the total accommodation for them. Supposing it found that there is still an excess of places, by no means follows that a town is well .Chooled; for there may be great excess 111 one area and great deficiency in another. There is, too, the religious diffi- 921tY. There might be ample accommodation 111 a Church school placed in a certain dis- trict, while the nearest Roman Catholic jachool might be overflowing; but it wouldn't be satisfactory to the Catholics to he told that they could send their children to the ,Church school. Nor would Churchmen, the 'conditions being reversed, like to send their -children to a Roman Catholic school. This is one of the disadvantages of denomi- ' tational schools; they seek to serve sec- tarian rather than public ends. Once let a ti.eCt get possession of an area, and it holds it, Or a time at any rate, to the exclusion of 'Zvery other sect. This cannot be said of '6oard Schools; they are built by the rate- Payers purely in the interests of the rate- , PaYers ; and, as there is no sectarian teach- 'g in them, they meet the wants of the ratepayers better than denominational schools fl possibly do. Board Schools require, of ,course, to be paid for, and for that matter 'he same may be said of denominational s„chools ; but in the latter case the attack on 'Lle pocket is a private attack, and it is nfined to a comparatively small section of the community. A School Attendance Com- Ipittee can work cheaply, but it cannot work !or nothing.; for, as Dr. MACKIE reminded the Council, the Committee and the Board of guardians spend between them some £6OO a Year. This is over one penny in the pound On the rates, and there is no Board School to show for it. Haying regard to the r lact that this £6OO represents the har- .4sing and the worrying of a large !lumber of poor parents, we are quite 'll accord with Dr. MACKIE in looking for- ward to free tuition as a means of getting rid 'r a bad element in our otherwise good sYstem of compulsory education. Alder- -111, an WEBSTER observes that the parents Ttranoned are "simply incorrigible," and that they are never brought before the magi- rates unless they have been before the `4oramittee at least twice. "Ay, there's the rub ; " they are really summoned three times; twice before the Corn- ttn,ittee, and then they are dragged before .ce magistrates—as though they were crim- 14als: And perhaps they are, for what greater offence can a man commit than to e poor? Dimes and dollars, dollars and dimes, A , An empty pocket's the worst of crimes. FAerman WEnsmit is not 'lacking in kindly eeling, but he takes a narrow view of edu- 4.etion, as is shown by his reference to half- 'liners, and his suggestion that the school aRe of children should be reduced. If he is peaking on behalf of the Committee in say- Li,that it is their opinion that "half-timers ~ :Tight safely be abolished," all we can say is ‘t'at the Committee have .committed them- elves to an unwise proposition. In many ; ancashire towns the half-timers, while earn- ‘ng their school fees and something towards

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: their keep, are the mainstay of the school : and, singular as it may seem, it has been found that in the matter of education they are rather above than below the average of the whole country. The half-time system is a good one ; it is because there are compai a- tively few half-timers in Warrington that its merits are not perceived. As to lessening the school life of children, that is quite out of the question. The highest authorities are agreed that it is a weak point of the present system, especially as revealed in our manu- facturing districts, that children are taken away from school too early. Just when they are getting to an age when rapid progress can be made, they are taken from school, and the chance is lost of their obtaining that special knowledge which goes to make the class of artizans of which England at the present moment stands so much in need. Let Aide:- man WEBSTER turn to the reports of the Committee of Council on Education, and he will find that the lament is not that children are kept at school too long, but that they are taken away too soon. He must elevate his vision; he, unfortunately, like the majority of people in towns where there are no School Boards, is behind in matters educational —he requires educating.

div.head: IMMMI
div.p: IMMMI

It appears that there is, after all, some foundation for what has been referred to as the " Cheshire Burial Scandal." Answering a question put by Mr. CARVELL WILLIAMS in the House of Commons last night week, Mr, CHILDERS denied, on the antbority of the Rev.. Canon COOPER, rector of Tarporlev, that there had been any undue interference in the case in questinn ; and it was added that the Rev. R. CHARLESWORTH, Wesleyan minister, and father of the child, was per- fectly satisfied with everything that was done. One story is good till another is told. Mr. CHARLESWORTH now gives his version of the facts, supported by the correspondence he has had with the Rector, and it is evident, to say the least of it. that he is anything but "perfectly satisfied" with what has been done. It seems that when the Wesleyan Minister gave the required notice, on the death of his child, that he purposed availing himself of the provisions ofl the Burials Act, Canon COOPER expressed himself as "much distressed" that he should think of such a thing; it would be a great grief to "the child's grandfather" anb then "all these years there has existed right order in Tarporley." The Canon's notion of "right order" would seem to be that people should forego their rights at his wish; and that a parent should think less of his own feelings than of his child'.s grandfather's. Mr. CHARLESWORTH declining to withdraw the 'notice, for reasons which he respectfully submitted, the Rector took care to suggest that any service that might be performed should be " Christian and orderly." Not knowing much about the ways of Wesleyan Ministers, he doubtless concluded that, if he did not see to it, the Rev. RICHARD CHARLESWORTH might inter his child in a manner that was unchristian and disorderly. But he did more than give a hint; he added :—" I must enter my pro- test, as this is the first time such a thing has ' been done here, against this violation of the rights of the Church and the feelings of Churchmen." The feelings of Dissenters are evidently nothing Li such a matter—so we may set aside that element in the case. But what of their rights? Does the law, or does it not, entitle them to inter in parish churchyards? If Mr. CHARLES- WORTH was not exceeding the law, and there is not a shred of evidence that he was, it was a piece of impertinence—it was unchristian and disorderly—on the part of Canon COOPER —IO make a protest, or to seek to interfere in any way. The Rector, as a servant of the State, ought to have done all he could to facilitate the carrying out of the law. If he will protest, let him protest against the Legis- lature, and if he is sufficiently in earnest let him do it by leaving a Sate Church which has so little regard for his ideas of what is "Christian and orderly" as to permit of Wesleyans being interred, with their own ervice, in the parish churchyard. Canon COOPER is evidently a Churchman of the good old school and he feels how much he is fettered by the State when he cannot ride roughshod over a Dissenter in the good old fashioned style.

M. GLADSTONE has presented his scheme for the better government of Ireland, and to- day it is the talk of both hemispheres. It is curious to note how completely "out of it," in some respects, many of the specuWions have been. There were few who were pre- pared for the proposal that Irish members of Parliament, in being granted legislative powers in Dublin, should be excluded from the Imperial Parliament in London, and yet it forms a cardinal feature of the scheme. This idea, if we mistake not, will ultimately be fathered upon the present Irish Secretary. It is, at any rate, certain that he has pre- viously advocated a plan of this kind. It now remains to be seen whether it can be carried out—or, perhaps, we should say whether it will prove acceptable to the Irish Nationalists. If they are likely to be con- tent with confining themselves to domestic legislation. England will be prepared to pay a high price to be left free from a pressure which at present paralyses the British Parliament. If, on the other hand, we are to have Irish M.P's. troop- ing to Westminster whenever they see a chance of getting one or other of the great English parties to bid for their votes, it be- comes a serious question whether it will be worth while to grant a separate Parliament for Ireland, A great deal, we anticipate, Wtll turn on this feature of thc; scheme the problem being to satisfy Ireland with Home Rule and Home Rule alone. The scheme is so large in its conception, and so hedged in with details which require great considera- tion, that we shall not emulate some of our contemporaries by deciding upon it first and thinking about it afterwards. It is as wide of the mark to speak of it as involving absolute separation as it is to•go to the other extreme and describe it, as Mr. MARRIorr does, as a scheme which does not confer half the powers possessed by the Metropolitan Board of Works. Whether it be approved or not, it cannot be denied that it is the outcome of the mature thought of the greatest states- man of modern times, and that, as such, it is entitled to the calm and dispassionate consideration of the people of Great Britain and Ireland.

- CRIME IN LA.NCASIIIRE.—The Chief Constable of Lancashire on Wednesday issued his quarterly re- port, showing that the number of apprehensions had i been 3,520, compared with 4,577 n the correspond- ing quarter of last year. The summonses by the police have been 4,610, a decrease of 430 on the cor- responding quarter of last year. The summonses by the parish au horities and others have been 677 more than the preceding quarters

div.head: F,XAAIINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 10, 1886
div.p: THE F,XAAIINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 10, 1886
"TOUCH AND GO."
just now, all the world is not a stage, but a Football Field. "Well done, Warring- ton !" and " Well done, Runcorn, too !" The play showed that both teams had educated their feet to some purpose.

The cutting of the first sod of a new col- liery at Golborne is a cheering performance. Let us hope that "tlye find" will be a royal one —not too much burdened with royalties—and that it will be a god send alike for master and man.

There has been a heavy poll at the Widnes Local Board Election. The fight has been hard, but no blood—bad or other- wise—has been spilt. It is pleasant to see victor and vanquished dwelling together in harmony, as they did at the close of the poll on Wednesday.

The Rev. T. R. Matthews has at length been " brought to " on the question of appointing managers for the EarlestoNvn Dis- trict School. It is due to Mr. J. E. Wors- ley, law clerk to the Newton Commissioners, to say that he would have been worsted if he had not displayed great tact, patience, and determination.

The Town Council are taking the right course in setting about a sub-division of the wards for polling purposes. There is always too much friction during a contested elec- tion, and if alterations can be made whereby the electors can record their votes easily and quickly, and without having to go far, it will be so much the better for them and every- body else.

The Warrington Farmers' Club has made its existence felt in more ways than one, but in one way especially. It is stated that the action which it has taken has resulted in re- missions of rent amounting .to no less than R+o,ooo. Tne Journal of the Club which has been published is a book of over xoo pages, and contains much that farmers will find interesting and valuable.

A Runcorn fish-dealer named John Morris has been fined ss. and costs for impeding Dr. McDougall, the Medical Officer Of Health, in the performance of his duty. The fishman eyed the doctor (while the doctor eyed the fish), and then suggested to his wife that she should " chuck a fish in his eyes." This was going a little too far; it was worse than proposing t 3 play chuck-farthing, for it cost John Morris 240 pence.

John 'Mather, of the Rose and Crown, Warrington, was tenderly dealt with in having a fine of [5 and costs only to pay for permit- ting betting on his premises. Granted that the informant was vindictive, that surely did not whitewash the defendant. The Mayor said there was "a somewhat discreditable element in the case." Of course; there always is in these betting transactions ; and that is why the law provides for heavy penalties.

Barrow Election is cold comfort for the Tories; they cannot, turn the figures as they will, make it appear, as they sometimes try to do; that, although they have lost, they ought to have won. Mr. Caine, who was a member of the last Gladstone Ministry, polled 151 more votes than Mr, Duncan, the Liberal candi- date at the General Election; whilst the Conservatives have polled 438 less. Our PD. says that a majority of g 35 is like corn- ing in with a whole team and a Barrowful under the waggon.

Mr. Seton-Karr was " talking at large" in the House of Commons on Friday evening, in the direction of Protection. He contends that we are living in a fool's paradise in the matter of trade. Most people would say that the state of trade is suggestive rather of pur- gatory than patadise ; but the member for St. Helens would seem to think he is privi- leged to talk nonsense on the question of "encouraging British industry." be has only a short innings as M.P., End he is trying, in his way, to make the most ot it.

Attention has been called in Parliament to the fact that there is an increase in the number of foreign seamen in the British merchant service, and inquiry is being made into the matter. Mr. Mundella said the foreign seam en,came principally from. Sweden,Norway, and Denmark, where the depression of trade is very great. What do the Fair Traders make of this..? If Great Britain is going to the dogs consequent upon a Free Trade policy, how is it that these foreigners cannot, at any rate. find sufficient to do to keep them going at home? Are they not sufficiently. "protected 9"

It is very easy to have too much of " Pro-. tection." There is a grandmotherly bill before Parliament which has for its •object the abolition of female labour on pit banks. It is designed to protect females.; but, as might be expected, the women who are likely to be affected object to be protected out of the right to earn a living in this par- ticular way. A meeting has just been held in St. Helens, from which it would seem that there is a strong feeling on the pit hanks against the proposal to prohibit female labour. Whilst women are gaining their rights in one direction, they must have a care that they are not deprived of them in another.
LOCAL NEWS.

TELE RET. W. GRLLLY AT RUNCORN.—On Sunday the Rev. W. Grelley, of Northwich, preached two sermons in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn. On Monday night Mr. Gelley delivered a lecture On "Gold in the gutter; or life on the street'," in which he dealt with the necessity for moral and social reforms. In the absence of Mr. Jas. Hand- ley. J.P., Mr. Wilkinson presided. FUNERAL OF A SUNDAY SCIIOOL TEACHER AT RUNCORN. —The funeral of Miss Jane Humphreys, daughter of the late Mr. John Humphreys, took place on Saturday after- noon in the Runcorn Cemetery. The deceased lady suc- cumbed to a painful and lingering illness on Wednesday at the age of 27 years. Miss Humphreys was trained for a schoolmistress at the Wesleyan Day School. She never, however, followed her avocation, but devoted her abilities in religious work in connection with St. John's Presbyterian Sunday School and Church, where her labours were very highly appreciated. In addition to being a teacher, she at one peeed was the organist of the church. The funeral was attended by many of the members and congregation of the chapel, by whom the loss of so valued a Christian worker I will be seyere:y felt. The hea-se was preceded by the Revs. E. Williams, R. P. Borwick, and E. Jones ; Dr. -Carruthers, Mr. James Pritchard, Mr. James Kirkham, Mr. John Prit- chard, Mr. D. H. Jones, Mr. Jackson, and many of the male and female Vachers of the Sunday schcol. The laxly was followed to the grave by Mr. John Humphreys, Mr. Robert Harrop, Mr. James Richardson, Mr. J. E. Warburton, Mr. Hugh Humphreys, Mr. Cotterill, Mr. John Wilton, Mr. R. G. Wilton, Mr. Cbatterton, Mr. Lays, and Mr W. Jepson. Wreaths were sent by Mrs. Hughes, of Llangefni ; Miss Chatterton, Miss James, and Miss Sareeant, Mr. James Richardson, Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst, Mr. J. W. Woodland, Miss Williams, Miss White (Stirling), and Miss E. Kirk- ham. Wreaths were also carried to the cemetery, and there placed on the coffin, by the members of the Sunday school class of the deceased, whose sad faces told how keenly they felt their loss. The body was borne from the hearse by the following teachers of St. John's Sunday school :—Messrs. F. Hewitt, R. Baxter, Richard Evans, R Leyland, Robert Evans, and M. Thomas. The service was conducted by the Rev. E. Williams, in the presence of a large number of spec- - tators.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.— The members on Thursday evening gave an excellent entertainment in Regent-street School. There was a fair attendance. COLONEL ASHTON, OF RueinonN —Friday night's " Lor- don G-,zette" announces that LienteColonel J. Ashton, of the 2nd C.R.V. (Earl of Cheater's Belles) has been granted the honorary rank of colcnel. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, Wrrneos —The Bey. R Yeatman's special sermons still succeed in drawing good congregations. On Sunday the titles of his discaerses were "The Great Teacher" and "Behold the Lamb." WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, W FIA.—Mr. T. Cottinghatn Edwards-Moss, M.P., has contributed £5 to a sale of work to be held shortly in aid of the reduction of the deist upon Moor-lane Welsh Congre7atiOnal Chapel, Widnes. THE COURT ,MINSTRELS.—This famous troupe of min- strels will occupy Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday and %Wednesday evenings next. The excellencies of their en- tertainment are well known, and good attendances may be anteeirested. 'ENGLAND 100 YEARS AGO."—On Monday evening the Rev. J. Colwell, of Liverpool, will lecture on this sub- ject in Lacey-street schoolroom, in aid of the fund for pro- viding a Wesleyan reading-room. Further particular 3 in eur advertisine. columns. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—The members of the juvenile branch gave an entertainment in the National School on Thursday evening, when a large audience assembled. The Vicar pr:- sided. The proceeds were in aid of the widow and family of a late member of the society. SACRED CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Frein our advertising celumns it will be seen that the members of the Runcorn Parish Church Glee Class, who have had a very successful season, will give a sacred concert on Thursday next. An excellent prograrntne has been arranged. THE PROPOSED INFECTIOUS DIsEaSES HOSPITAL FOR W'DNES —After considerable delay the Local Government Board have at last intimated their selection to the piens of the Widnes Local Board for the erection of ate iefectious diseases hospital. No doubt the work will be pushed on as rapidly as possible. , PROPERTY SALE AT WIDNES.—Mr. Barnett Dutton, axe- ' tioneer, on Thursday evening offered for sale at the Central 1 Hotel several lots of property in Viaduct-street. Widner, Windermere and Church-streets, Farnworth, and Elizabeth- terrace, Ditton. The reserve price was not „reached in any instance, and all the lots were withdrawn. CAMRRIDGFI LOCAL EXAMINATIONS—The order sf merit as regards those students who gained the mark of distinc- tion in the late examinations of the Cambridge Univeisity Local Eximinetione Syndicate has been issued From the list we gather that Miss C. Handley, daughter of Mr. Jamee Handley, J.P., has passed first in French, with the mark of distinction. FOOTB&LL AT WIDNES —On Thursday a football match was played at Widnes between a team from the works of Messrs. Gossage and Son, and another from the works of the Widnes Alkali Company. After a hard game the Alkali team won by 2 goals, 2 tries, and 7 minors to 1 goal. 1 try. and 4 minors. The same day a frieadly match was also, played between the first team of the eVidnes Recreation Club and eighteen of the second team. ADDRESSES TO WO4KING-MEN AT WIDNES.—The Rev. R. G. Hughes, of the Milton Congregational Church, Widnes. on Sunday commenced a series of Sunday evening addresses to working-men and their wives. There was a moderately good congregation. "Three things working-men ought to be familiar with " was the title of the discourse, which was both practical and interesting. The "things " were— How to keep their health, how to enjoy their homes, and a good conscience. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—Mr. T. Cottingham Edwards-Moss, M.P.. will open a hazer at this place of worship on Wednesday afternoon next. At- pre,esr the Sunday school and divine service have to be conducted in the earns building, and frequently much discomfort and inconvenience is caused in consequence. The congregation have started a fund for the laudable object of building a new school, and the bazaar, which gives promise of being a success, is intend, d to augment that fund. MISSIONARY SERMONS AT FARNWORTIL—The Bev. F. Bellamy, missionary from the Holy Lend. occupied the pulpit at St. Lake's Church, Farnworth, on Sunday morn- ing and evening, and in the afternoon at 3 o'clock he preaelied in Bold Schoolroom. On Alonday evening a public meeting was held at Farnworth, when the same gentleman delivered an interesting address, giving his ex- periences as a missionary in the Holy Land. A collection was made on behalf of the society at each of the Sunday services. There were good congregations. DEATH OF MRS. HALLOWS AT DITCON.—Death has re- ' centiv removed an old resident of Ditton, at the age of 93, in the person of Mrs. Hallows. Up to the last the old lady had full possession of all her faculties, and as an instance of her activity we may state that in June last she knitted six pairs of garters for the Ditton Church bazaar. She formerly resided in Preston, and was a descendant of the family of Macintosh, of Inverness, which took a pro- minent part in the Scottish Rebellion of 1715. Her mother lived to be a centenarian. Mrs. Hallows will be missed in Ditton. BETHESDA CHAPEL. RIINCOWN.—Tinder the auspices of the Ladies" Sewing Class of this Place of worship, a mis- cellaneous entertainment was given in the schoolroom on Monday evening. There was a numerous attendance. A capital programme commenced with a magic lantern exhi- bition, the gentlemen in charge being Messrs. W. Rhodes, I. Rhodes. and H. W. Handley. A vocal and • instru- mental concert followed, and was attended with much sec- cess. The Misses Handley, Simkin, and E. Crosby ; Meets. Joule, F. Scott, and E. Rhodes took part. MissF. Handley was the accompanist. Tug RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.—A cash statement of the Runcorn Free Public Library Committee was presented to the Board of Commissioners at the last monthly meeting. The receipts included £172 3s 61 from the rate; fines, is 2d; borrowers tickets, £6 3s 6d; donation, £5, and other small items; total, £228 121 s ld. he expenditure included salary of librarian and secretary, £5O; magazines and periodicals. £2O 44 31; new books, £7O Ise 4.1; binding hooks. £l4 16s 61; rent, cleaning, lighting, and heating, 'arc., £25; making a total expenditure of £193 Os 81 There was a balance in hand of £35 73 sd. SAD ACCIDENT TO AN OLD WOMAN AT WIDNES.—An old woman, aged 64, the wife of William Retcliffe, of 8, Ger- rard-street, West Bank, Widnes, met with a serious accident on Monday at noon. The unfortunate woman was taking her husband's dinner to Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co's. Works, and in her harry to accomplish the journey she went beneath a wagon on West Bank Dock, forming part of a -train. She arrived safely ou the other side, but she stooped and reached forth her arm to pick up the dinner, which she had placed on the ground under the wagon: At that mo- ment the train moved and a wheel passed over the limb and completely shattered it. She was cenveyed in a cab to the Accident Hospital, where her arm was amputated by Drs. McDonnell and McCambridge. The woman had been pre- viously warned against going under wagons by several of the workmen. FREE DINNER MOVEMENT AT WIONES. -- This move- naent, which commenced eleven weeks ago, bas been the means of providing 6,000 dinners to children of poor par- ents. The dinners have been given to the children of widows and to those whose fathers were sick or out of work The teachers at the various elementary scheols have super- intended the catering with sympathetic interest. On Thursday night a service of gong entitled " Billy Bray " was given in the Lacey-street schoolroom, Widnes, on be- half of the movement. There was a moderete attendance. Mr. W. Clarke occupied the chair, and the narrative was read by Mr. Robert Cook. The service was organised 'ley the members ref the Ditton Young Men's Mutual Improve- ment Society, the conductor being Mr. John Davies, and the accompanist Miss Peover, of (Afton. The service was well rendered under Mr. Davies' direction, and at the close the choir were awarded a unanimous vote of thanks. Mr. S. B. Stringer gave a brief sketch of the free dinner move- ment, and mentioned some interesting incidents in its his- tory. Votes of thanks were passed to the chairman and te Mr. Cook, and the proceedings closed. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD FINANCES.— A special meeting of Widnes School Board was held on Thursday afternoon 'for the purpose of signing the balance sheet for the half- year ended the 25th March. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided, and there were present—the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, and Denby (clerk.) It appeared that the half-year was commenced with a bal- ance of £1,244 13s Id. the receipts included grants from the Committee of Council on Education, and Science, and Art Department £2,195 63 2d, and school fees £823 10, 54. Including the balance, the receipts amounted to £4,292 6s 21. The expenditure amounted t 4 £3,625 Os 61, leaving a balance of £667 5s 84. The salaries of officers of the Board amounted to £225, legal and other expenses of administra- tion £69 Os sd, salaries of teachers £1,799 17s, b 'ohs, ap- paratus, and stationery £55 3s 51, furniture and repairs £268 4s 11d, other expenses of maintenance £6O. The total cost of maintaing the sehools was £2,183 12s 14. The out- standing liabilities of the Board amount to £32.720 14s 3d, borrowed from the Public Works Loan Commissioners.

On the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe. seconded by the Chairman, the balance sheet was approved. CONCERT AT ST. BEDE'S RONAN CATHOLTC CHURCH, APPLETON.—The seventh and last concert of the season in connection with this church was given in the new echool- room on Monday night to a large and appreciative audi- ence. Where one and all of the performers acted their re- sp-ctive parts so well it would be invidious to particularise. Suffice to say that Miss Leatherbarrow, Miss Johnston, anHdaMyeesssarsn.dMcoromrispoinnyansdintl,2ianyg„ es fully Minstrelymaintaineßdeyth.,e,ir The brought ro o re- putationsght taos o first-classve ry pl vocalists,eosaot on dan d satisfactoryo f - juniorthe cl close amateurs . we cannot omit to mention Miss Jameson, whose tasteful rendering of " Dermot Asthore " and "Susie " fairly en- raptured the audience. In a humourons duet with Mr. Finn she acted her part with a modest self-composure and preci- sion not often met with even in a professional. Mr. Finn acqnitted himself very creditably in the duet with Miss Jameson, and also in the Irish song" My Eileen Asthore," which he sang with remarkable correctness and pathos. He deservedly obtained an encore on both occasions. Miss Oak- den sang the Scotch song. " Within a mile of Edinbro' 1 oon," with very good effect, considering the difficulty an English lady must feel in pronouncing the Scotch version, and in response to an encore she sang "Just to please the boys." The comic element was very ably sustained by Dr. McCambridge, and Messrs. Finn and Davies. We regret that we have not more opportunities of hearing Dr. Mc- Cambridge, who gives truly humourous renderings of his songs. Miss Cullen presided at the pianoforte with her usual good taste and ability. After a vote of thanks to the singers, proposed by Father Finnegan, the concert was , object of these concerts was to liquidate the debt on the echools.

17 ASSAULT AT Itroteccore.—At the Cheshire Quarter Ses- sions, held at Knutsford, on Tuesday, Henry Alldritt, on bail, was indicted for assaulting Fanner Morrell, at Runcorn, on the 21st January, 1886. —Mr. E. H. Lloyd prosecuted. and Mr. Marehall defended.—Prisouer was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. LICENSING MATTERS AT RUNCORN. —Ooloncla.y, at Run- corn Petty Sessions, John Coxhill was eranted a tea:Tor- arty authority te sell at the Greenway Vauits Hotel, now kept by Elizabeth Chadwick.—Similar authority was gran- ted to Joseph Grundy to sell at the Nlasonic Hotel, and to Bendict B. Birchen to sell at the Royal •Oak Inn. Weston, lately kept by Phcebe Barrow. INCREASED POOR RATE FOR WIDNES —A new poor rate of 2e 4d in the pound was signed by the magietrates (Messrs. E. K. Muspratt and John Brock), at the Widnee Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday. *Mr. Goff, Resistant-overseer, said the Lest rate was 2e in the pound, and the whole of it bad been collected with the exception of £25 arrears. That, how- ever, was recoverable. It was estimated that the new rate would produce the sum of £14,997, and it was owing largely to the increased expenditure which had to be met, and to reduced aesessments, that the extra 41 had been put on. POLICE INSPECTION AT WIDNES.—Captain the Hon. C. G. Legge, the Government inspector for the Northern Divi- sion, held an inspection of the police in the sub-division of Widnes on Wednesday afternoon in the Drill Hall. He was accompenied by Colonel Moorsom, the chief constable for Lancashire, and Superintendent Barker. Theite were pre- sent, Inspector Wood, five sergeants, and 31 constables. Th,ee constables were on duty. The iuspector examined the clothing and appointments of the men, and pnt them through a course of drill. He afterwards inspected the looks, and appeared to be thoroughly satisfied with every- taing be bad seen. Acrecre AGAINST A SurroN FARMER.—At Runcorn Petty Seseions, on Monday, Samuel Roberts, a labourer, sued William Grounds, farmer. Aston-by-Sutton, for £7 10e, alleged to be aratees doe under a contract. Mr. W. H. Linaker defended. From the complainaet's statement it appeared that he was engaged for 12 months, his wages to be £lB. On the 30th March, Mr. Grounds put his fist on the complainant's jaw. and said if" he was not out he would knock tii out." He went, and although he had only worked a quarter. he wished for six months' wages "if he could get therm"—Mr. Linaker said Mr. Grounds was willing to pay the complainant a quarter's wages and ! rake him iHck.--,-bocriplainant agreed to this course, and I the Bench made the necessary order. The coots of thel cowrt were divided. UNWEIGHED. BREAD AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty • • Sessions, on Monday, Francis Lawrinson, grocer, High- street, was summened for selling bread without previously weighing it. Mr. T. J. Peters, solicitor, Widnes, de`eeded.l' It was alleged that a girl, sent into the defendant's shop • • by P.C. Smith. asked for three 41b. loaves, which were . supplied by a boy named Clarke for 3d each. The boy , • dici not weieh the bread. Eacn loaf weighed about 31lbe. —Mr. Peters pointed out that there was a notice in the shop that bread was sold at id per lb , and it. was the de• fendant's custom to m Ike loaves 3X-lbs. in weight for 3!ad. i The loaves averaged, however, %lbs. He contended that the statute had not been infringed a§ the defencl,mt was per- fectly willing to weigh the bread if asked. He called two witnesset to support his statement, and one stat,d the girl only asked for a IJ:reed:me9 halfpenny loif.—The Bench considered there had been a breach of the law, but not a flaqrant one, and imoesed a fine of 5s and costs, 20s. ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Catherine Cunningham. a tramp, was charged with stealing from the person of Charles Simmons, eneine driver, 29, Albert-road, Widnes, the sum of 6s GI On the afternoon of the 29 le March Simmons paid for he prisoner 1 several glaesee of, beer. She went and sat besides him, and he caught her alhtracting money from his pocket. She ; placed some of he money in Per mouth. She pleaded euilto, and was senti aced t.) a month's hard labour --1 Herriet Ball, a young woman, was charged with having on • Saturday, the 27th March, stolen a jacket-bodice and a skirt, value 3s 91, the property of Robert Frederick Little- weed, a second-hand clothes dealer, of Warrington. The oroseceter's wife had a stall in the Market, and the prisoner bought several small articles there, but not those in ques- tion, which were missed shortly after her departure. On . Saturday, the 3rd April, Mrs. Cunnah, a woman who ! lodged with the prisoner in Peasant-street was seen wearing the skirt and bodice, and inquiries showed that she had pur- chased them from the prisoner for is Bd.—lnspector Wood • said the prisoner had been convicted for drunkenness and breach of the peace. Her husband was. an industrious man. The prisoner, who protested that she found the articles on the ground near a sweet stall," was fined 30s or 14 days' imprisonment.--Win. Jones, a young man, was charged with stealing a tablespoon worth 2cl from the dining-rooms : of Mrs. Unewortin Victoria-road. On Saturday night the prisoner had some soup at .the rooms, and Mrs. Unsworth missed one of the spoons. The prisoner, who was in drink, said he bad not seen it, but she searched him end found the article in his trou,er pocket. She had missed six spoons t that day.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. DR. IMCMCCGALL AND THE FISH DEALER.—John Morris, fish dealer, Water-street, was summoned at Runcorn Police ! Court on Monday charged with having on the 27th March . unlawfully impeded Dr. McDougall, the medicel officer of health to the Board of Commissioners, in cerrying out the provisions etf the Public Health Act, 1875.—The defendant • pleaded guilty.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared to prosecute, and read the sections of the Act empowering the medical of- tmer to inspect fish and food of all descriptions, and pointed , out that the penalty for impeding him in his duty was £5 —Dr. McDougall stated that on Saturday afternoon, the . 27th ult., an intimation was sent to him that bad meat WAS being exposed in the market for sale. He advised his in- ! formant that the proper course would be to take possession of the meat, but he was unable to do so as the ineat had been removed. As the time was drawing nigh, when choleret and other diseases might be expected. it would be necessary to exercise every conceivable supervision over the food of the people; and on Saturday night about 8 o'clock he went , round the stalls at the market. On the defendant's stall he ' found some fish exposed for sale, and which appeared to him to require a little locking after. It was, however, not in that 'condition that he felt it incnmbent upon him to seize it. He was of op'nion it was fit for the food of man. He asked the defendant to bring a light which he bed at one end of the -stall to bear upon the fish. The defendant began to be very abusive, and at last be told his wife that she had better "chuck a fish in his eyes." The defendant knew well that. he (witness) was the medical officer of health..—The defen- dant said when the doctor came up there were about 40 people round u.,n T d the stall, pspteaoll,lae beganndsaid "Stop, stop, what's this you are to go away. and lie told his • wife to wrap the doctor a fish up and let him take it saway, She did so. hut he would not take it, so he (defendant) said 4' throw it after him if be does not take it." He denied that he told his wife to send a fish in the doctor's face.—The Bench imposed a fine of 53 and costs. 20s. TIIE SHIP CANAL BILL.—The .Corporation of Liverpool have again presented a petition to the , -House of Lords praying to be heard against • the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. No day has yet been • named for submitting the Bill to the examiners. WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY CHALLENGE CUP.— The- final tie in the above competition will be played on the Liverpool College Cricket Ground, Fairfield, to-day (Saturday), between Warrington and Aspull, kick-off at 3-30. Umpires, Me.ssrs.'l Wilcock (Wa,vertree) and J. Williams (Bootle) •'I referee, Mr. A. T. Kemble (Liverpool). The pro.: ceeds will be devoted to charitable institu- tions. The challenge cup will be presented on the ground. The following are the teams : Warrington: Buxton, back; .Tolley, Barnes, and Boardman, three-quarter backs ; Gilbert and Speakman, half backs; Fair. Turner, P. Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Davies, Povey, Rigby, Ashton (captain), and W. Heyes, forwards. Aspull : Paw- her,, back;' J. Roberts (captain), It. Seddon, and J. . Samuels, three-quarter backs; D. Hulme and Cartwright, half backs ; Hampson, Hesketh, Bram- well, Monks, Ha,ydock, Lawson, Lindsay, Brooks, and Pilkington, forwards. Much enthusiasm is manifested in 'Warrington regal ding the event, and there is no doubt that a large contingent of War- rinc,donians will take advantage of the cheap trains to Liverpool to witness the match. DARESTIURY HIG ['WAY BOARD.—A mee,tin,g• of. this Board was held in the Court Room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. E. Greenall (chair- man) presided, and there was a good attendance of members.—Lumb Brook Bridge : The Clerk (Mr. Linaker) read some correspondence which had taken place between him and the Bridgewater Navi- gation Co. with respect to the maintenance of the road at the above bridge, and from which it ap- peared that the company had decided to continue to maintain the road.—A Complaint : A letter was read from Mr. It. Davies, calling attention to the " fright- ful state of the road at Wilderspool, especially oppo- site the new cottages being built for the brewery." It was stated, however, that the road in question was not under the Board's charge, and the- Clerk said he had informed Mr. Davies to this effect.—Thc Steam Roller ...The Chairman said the committee ap- pointed to consider the question of obtaining a steam roller had no report to make. They had had a meeting that morning at which they appointed a a small sub-committee to see the surveyor of the Warrington district in which they had been using a steam roller for some time, and the committee would report at the next meeting,.—Contracts : It was agreed to accept the tenders of Messrs. Neshaw, Lupton, and Co.; Messrs. Darbyshire and Co. ; and Messrs. Nunnerley and Co. for broken stories to be delivered at various points in the Board's district. —The Rate : The Surveyor submitted his estimate of expenditure for the ensuing year, and after this had been considered and adopted the Clerk stated that the total call which would be reoired from the overseers of the various townships would amount to £1,776 (Is sd. A 3d rate would there- fore give £6O more than they wanted. (Hear, hear.) The clerk was instructed to prepare precepts to be served on the various overseers.—Complimen- tary : This being the last meeting of the Board as at present constituted, a cordial vote of thanks was, on the motion of Mr. Mclntyre, passed to the chair- . man.—The Meeting then terminated.

THE Misstox.—The ten days' mission which has been. conducted by the Rev. T. R. Willacy, vicar of Thorganby, has just been concluded. It was a very successful one, addresses having been given by geatlemen interested in the object in various cutting shops in the village, and many well attended services having been held. The mission has been assisted by the Rev. H. A. D. Surridge, vicar of High Legh, the Rev. C. F. Rogers, organising secretary of the National Society, and the Rev. E \Y. Lomax. LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—Mr. J. D. Dewbursf, the re- turning officer, made known the result of this election on Saturday afternoon. It was as follows :—Mr. Hugh Cameron' agent, The Chestnuts, Lymm, 528 votes; Mr., ; William BrazEndala, builder. Bridgewater-street, Lymm, 501 votes; Mr. John Thomason. beotmaker, Bank Cottage.. , Bridgeivat.r. street, Lymm, 464; Mr. Daniel Rogers' com- mission agent, Statham, Lymm, 433; Mr. Frederick. Holt,. agent, The Cross, Lymm, 392; and Mr. Frederick Orlando I Meston, master fustian cutter, Mona Villa, Newfield, liVnun 288. The first three gentlemkt are elected. Mr. Braaendate is the only new member, and takes the place ot I Mr. Rogers.

div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Offices at Lymm on Thursday evening, when the chair was occepied by Mr. H. Cameron. There were also present Messrs. Thomason. Forster, Hall, Gibbons, Appleton, Ridgway (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical cfficer of health). THE HEALTH OF THE Mermen—Dr. Fox read a volu- minous report, to receive which was the object of calling the meeting. After referring at length to the subject of the preservation of life and to the uses of Sanitation, the Medi- cal Officer said that since the period reterred to in the last annual report great advance had been made in the sanitary position of Lymm. The arrangements for the removal of refuse had been placed on a more systematic and therefore satisfactory basis, and the influence of that beneficial change had appeared from year to year in the accounts of vital statistics. In order to estimate •fully the importance gf this department of sanitary work it had only to be consi- dered that zymotic, or idectiotre complaints, had the pecu- liarity that those suffering from them eked off during their illness materials chargedwith the disease. This showed the im- portance of houses, wherever possible, being connected with sewers. The vital statistics of Lymm for the year 1885 pre- sented the striking feature that in the absence of zymotic diseases in an epidemic form, the infantile mortality was- not below the average. The inference was that the infantile rate of mortrlity, and, therefore. t 3 a certain extent the general rate, was not controlled or limited by the absence or pre.ence of zymotic and epidemic disease in the district. During the year there were registered 150 blithe, and. 87 deaths at all ages and from all causes. This yielded an an- nualbirth rate of 31 6, against an average of 330. and an annual death rate of 18.3. Lymm had been exempt from the wave of measles that had passed over the country. There had been no deaths from that complaint since 1883. Still the intent& deaths were 33 in number, and comet'. tut,d 380 per cent.- of the entire mortality. The proportion was exactly the same as in 1881, when the death rate was 111, and the zymotic total repre- sented by a decimal iipte below 1 per 1000. Among the difficulties that should be present to the mind in a contemplation of vital statistics was the possible Pre- sence of an influential number of improvident people wiu se children were ready prepared and marked out to make :Ai early appearance in the bills of mortality. The remedy for this did not rest with the Board, Mat rather with the erni- series of religion and benevolence, who might be able to inspire and encourage habits of providence and domestic carefulness, by which means the condition of infant life might be ameliorated. This was Lymm's heavy drawback, made more plain by each year's accumulated statistics. Otherwise Lymm was healthful and beautiful, and should present statistics as favourable as any health resort in the kingdom.—The report was adopted on thlt moticn of Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. Appleton, and the Board soon after- wards rose.

WARRINGTON WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE- MENT SOCIETY.—On Tuesday evening a social gathering to celebrate the conclusion of a pre- eminently successful session 'was held in the Bold- street Schools. The Rev. J. Howell Jones occupied the chair, and after an able address from him the secretary read a very favourable report of the busi- ness of the past session, eulogising the services which the chairman had rendered to the society. During the ;evening, songs, recitations, &c., were rendered in an admirable manner by some of the members and frienda. Several curiosities and ob- jects of interest were on vie*, contributions having been lent by his Worship 'the Mayor (Jos. Harrison, Esq.) and the Warrington Field Club.

THE OLDEST ODDFELLOW.—The ".Odd.fellows' Magazine" says the oldest Oddfellow in the Man- chester Unity is BrO. Peter Bradley, who was ini- tiated in the Good Samaritan Lodge, Na. 19, Marple District, on the 16th January, 1816. He has been a member of the Order for more than seve,nty years, and although ninety-two years old, still attends the meetings or his lodge , CHESHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.—The 80th annual meeting of the Cheshire Congregational Union was held on Wednesday at Middlewich, Ander ' the presidency of Mr. Thomas Rigby. It appeared that the income of the Union had fallen off during the year, and it 'was not possible to send a contribu- tion to the Church Aid Society this year. An appeal was made for active help to make good this defi- ciency. During the meeting the relationship of Sunday schools to the Churches was discussed. Cheadle was fixed upon as the place of the next meeting. ' COLLIERY EXTENSION.—The interesting ceremony of cutting the first sod of the new colliery which Messrs. R. Evang and Co. are about to sink in con- -nection with their'plant at Golborne took place on Saturday afternoon in the presence of a large assembly. Among those present were the Rector and Mrs. Richardson, Mr. Arthur Evans (Haydock), and Mr. T. Drayton-Grimke, nephews to Mr. Joseph Evans, and Mr. B. B. Glover, agent to the firm, tozether with the principal officials connected with the Golborne, Edge Green, Haydock, and Parr Collieries. Mr. R. Yates, manager of Golborne Col- lieries. on behalf of Messrs. Evans and Co., pre- sented Mrs. Grimke with a handsome. spade, with which she cut the "first sod" amid loud cheeks. APPROACHING, MARRIAGE OF MR. SETON-KARR. —The marriage of Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens, which will take place towards the latter end of the present mcnth, will be made the occa- sion of a public presentation of an illuminated address, subscribed for by the Conservatives of St. Helens. A committee has been formed, and the preliminary arrangements are being made. A con- gratulatory meeting on a large scale .will probably be held in the Volunteer Hall about the 17th inst., and, if - parliamentary duties permit, Mr. Seton-Karr will be present to receive the address. The bride- elect is Miss Thorburu, of Edinburgh, who, we be- lieve. is related to Mrs. Wm. Gamble, a daughter- in-law of Colonel Gamble, Mr. Seton-Kares oppo- nent in the late election, and.is also connected with a well-known Liverpool family of her own name. It may be remembered that Mr. Seton-Karr lbst his first wife (a daughter of,Mr. William Pilkington, of Roby Hall) some two years ago.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

This annual contest concluded on Wednesday, when the counting of the votes took place at the offices ofVre Local Board, Alforde Ciaa.mbers. It was without any element of excitement. The only advocacy of the claims of the candi- dates were contained in their addresses which were pub- lished last week, and altogether the election may be des- cribed as tame. The counting commenced at nine o'clock in the Board-room. Mr. F. H. Gossage, chairman of the Board, was the returning officer, and he was assisted by Mr. C. H. Lewin, solicitor, as legal adviser. Mr. Goff, the , assistant overseer, was present to render any aid with the register of voters, and Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, was busily' engaged. The officials in the office (Messrs. Hoyle. Wilson, Whitfield, Heves, Sankey, and Hughes) were the countess. The interests of the candidates nominated by the Owners' and Occupiers' Association were watched by Messrs. J. W. Wareing, Joseph Morrison. T. Atherton, F. 1 immis, and W. Crabtree. Mr. T. Sadler acted en behalf of Mr. Midsvood, Mr. A. Manley for his brother, Mr. E. Martlev, Mr. J. W. Seymour for Mr. for- rabin, and Mr. W. Sadler for Mr. It. Webster. The candi- dates were present during the greater part of the day, and the proceedings passed off very pleasantly. There was a large number of papers returned blank, while for Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. Midwood there were many plurnpers. A "state of the poll" was issued at 12 noon and 3-15 p.m., and the result was declared at five o'clock as follows:— W. W. Gossage Dr. O'Keeffa 1,753 Ft. Webster J. Houghton J.Midwood B. 0•ok The result was posted on the window of the Examiner " Office (Mr. E. Martley's), and was read by a considerable number of people. Mr. W. W. Gossage, after the declaration, said he had the honour, being placed at the head of the poll, to propose a vote of thanks to the returning officer for the way in which he had conducted the business that day. He had done it in a most impartial manner, and no one could have done it better. Mr. Horabin seconded the motion.
He was happy to say

that Mr. F. H. Gossage had performed his oneroui-cluties in an honest and straightforward manner. He hoped ,next time he was a candidate be would run a little nearer the top. Had be and his colleagues (Messrs. Webster and Martley) put forth the same efforts as their opponents their position would have been much improved. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried by loud acclamation. Mr. F. H. Gressage said he had been returning officer he did not know bow many times, but he did not suppose he should be again. Thtrefore be had to tender his sincere thankg to all who had helped in carrying out the election, for their kind services whether voluntary or otherwise. The efficiency of the officials could not be doubted for a moment. They had, he believed, hall the heaviest poll ever made, and it spoke volumes for the assiduity, and honest purpose, and straightforwardness of those who had to count the votes that the result could be declared at five o'clock. He did not • kn.w whether it was in his provincao to mention such a fact, but he felt flattered by the reception his son had received. (Applause.) He could not help doing so. He thought he ought honestly, as returning officer, to congratulate Mr. Midwood at the position he occupied on the poll. • He had known Mr. Mid. wood individually, and as a member of the Board, for many years, and that the people of Widnes appreciated the ser- vices he had rendered to the town in the past was shown by the way in which they had recorded their votes. He trusted he would have health and strength to do his honest duty— (hear, hear,)—to the community. Mr. Webster, as one of the defeated candidate., thanked the returning officer, and said although on the losing side , now, he and his colleagues intended to be on the winning . side on another occasion. THE WELLINGTON FOOTBALL CHALLENGE CITP.—The matches in Vie first round of the competition for the Wel- lington Football Challenge Cup, at present held by the Earlestown F.C., last year's winners, were commenced on Saturday afternoon, when the following ties were played : Earlestortra (end) v. Sankey Refiners (Ist) : These teams met on the ground of the first named, the Mesnes, and there was a good number of spectators present. Excitement ran pretty high, and two players came to blows. The Earlestown 2nd team won by six goals to none.— Haydock Ramblers v.Larlestown Swifts.—Played on the ground of the former at Haydock, and resulted in the de- fog of the Swifts by four goals to none. Haydodk Wan- derers v. St. He!ens St. Mark's, —Played at Haydock, and the spectators witnessed a hard and even fought game. The Haydock eleven claimed the match by five goals to four. One of the points claimed by Haydock was disputed by their opponents. Stubshaw Cross Wanderers v. _Ashton Recreation (let). The tie between these terms excited a considerable amount of local feeling, but the Wanderers held the upper hand and won by four goals to one. The Recreation handed in a protest against the eligibility of one of the players for Stubshaw Cross —A meeting of the committee elected to hear protests was held at the Wellington Inn, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening, when it was decided that the pro- tests mentioned in the last two ties be upheld, and both matchks were ordered to be re-played. The remaining ties in the first round will be played off to-day (Saturday.)

NOTES BY THE WAY. The Earlestown Wanderers met the second team of the Blackburn Olympic on the ground of the first-named at Newton Common, on Saturday afternoon. A well-con- tested game resulted in the defeat of the visitors by three goals to one.

The final tie of the competition for the National Cup proved one of the most exciting struggles that has taken place on the Kennington Oval for a long period, and the prediction that the contest for supremacy would be close was verified. In the half-dozen ties previouslyplaved by each team, the aggregate score had been the same for each of the.rival clubs of Saturday, and this pointed to their quality. The result of the tie at the Oval confirmed the vies., for neither side could score an advantage over the other in the course of play, maintained with surprising vigour for an hour and a half. The general verdict on the match was that the West Bromwich Albion had somewhat the best of the play on the whole, and deserved victory. The Blackburn R ,vers were hooted by the supporters of the rAlbionites for declining to play for an.extra half hour, but the decision to defer the further test was good policy. This day (Saturday) the teams again meet at Derby. An unusual amount of excitement was created on Satur- day, when those local teams Runcorn and Warrington faced each other at Widnes in the semi-final of the West Lanca- shire Cup Tie. An assemblage of near 12,000 people sur- rounded the enclosure at the time advertised for the kick-off, and the sate realised near £l3O. The Runcorn captain fortunately won the toss, and placed his men with a very strong wind at their backs. The fine defensive play of the Warrington forwards during this half was a treat, keep- ing the leather very close in the pack, and carried almost every scrimmage. Twos minors to nil was the score at half time, and when ends were changed the Warrington sup- porters were very jubilant. In very quick time twe minors were scord, and Runcorn were penned on their line. An unfortunate matter took place that caused the match to be left in an unfinished state, though the referee awarded it to Warrington, as their opponents de- clined to continue the game. The Union Com- mittee meeting, held the same night, decided that the match, be replayed at Southport on Wednesday. The Warrington team made the journey at eleven a.m., ac- companied by a great number of supporters. They were first on the field of play, and were in splendid condition. Their white jerseys and pants looked very attractive. Four twentys were agreed upon, and the first one Warring- ton faced hill and wind, and at the expiration were nil to Runcorn 10. Minors rapidly succeeded each other, and Ashton got a try just at the call of time, the score standing 9to 10. In the third portion Runcorn scored 4to Warrington 1 try Speakman and 1 minor, making 14 all. Entering the last twenty, matters were very one-sided. Warrington record- ing 10 points to nil. One try Hayes, Speakman kicked a goal, 1 try F. Turner, and 4 minors. A very enthusiastic recep- tion was given to the team on their arrival home. Aspull have beaten St. Helens Recreation by 13 points to 4. The final takes place at Liverpool on Saturday, and should the Warrington team win a most flattering wel- come will be given them.
