The Central News telegraphs: th scene in the House of Commons this (Thursday) morning is one which has not been equalled during the present generation. The anxiety of members to hear Mr. Gladstone's statement to-night has reached the highest pitch, and has led them to make sacrifices of an unusual character to obtain seats for the all- important sitting. Before six o'clock this morning the House was besieged with Irish members, and by half-past six nearly the whole of the Irish con- tingent had arrived, and at once securedsll the best , seats both above and below the gangway on the Opposition side of the House. Mr. Henniker Heaton was the first Conservative to put in an appearance, at half-past seven, and was greeted by a hearty cheer from the early callers, much apparently to his astonishment. The first to secure a seat on the Liberal benches was Mr. Saunders, of East Hull, and the next arrival was Mr. King, the Conservative member for Central Hull. Each new arrival was cheered heartily by the Irishmen, until the proceed- ings became somewhat monotonous, and this fact dawning at length upon the representatives of Erin, they trooped off in a body to seek their early breakfast, leaving their hats to mark the seats they had taken. At half-past eight the dining-room was filled by a small but hungry army, who seemed prepared to do justice to a substantial breakfast after their unwonted experience of the invigorating morning air. Mr. Labouchere turned up at a quarter before nine o'clock, and secured his usual seat. By nine o'clock about one hundred and fifty members had taken their places, and from that hour the stream of arrivals was continuous. , In this connection the following figures may prove of interest six o'clock the number of members in the House was six, and at half-past six they sat 47; at eight, 56; at nine, 83; and at ten, 150. Mr. Cyril Flower, one of the Government whips, arrived shortly after nine, and Lord Arthur Hill, one of the Opposition whips, about ten. Several ladies came down at the latter hour to await the opening of the particular gallery. The floor of the House of Commons and the pre- cincts of the House gather in animation as the day advances, but a few of the very early ones are somewhat at a loss to kill time until the hour arrives for the assembling of the House. The joy- ous spirits of the Irish members, however, have proved equal to the occasion, and during the morn- ing several of them have taken exercise on the terrace of the Houses on a tricycle borrowed for the occasion from the manager of the. refreshment rooms. The fun was kept up fast and furiously, until at length Mr. P. J. O'Brien, M.P. for Tipper- ary, came to grief, the machine collapsing and sending the hon, member violently to the ground. He sustained a severe cut near the eye from con- tact with a sharp stone, and was taken off to the hospital by his friends to have the wound dressed. This put an end to the tricycle practice, and Mr. O'Brien, returning sometime afterwards from the surgeon's with his face and hand bandaged, became the centre of sympathetic interest. The crowd at half-past three in the afternoon far outstripped in number anything before seen at tlfe opening of the House for business, even upon the appearance of the Queen. Members continued to pass in unrecognised by the crowd. From the Houses of Parliament to Downing-street, the whole pathway was held by the crowd. Shortly before half-past four Mr. Gladstone, ac- companied by his wife, left Downing-street in an open carriage drawn by a single horse and escorted by a strong body of mounted police. Hearty cheers were at once raised which were heard and taken up by the crowd along the route. In Whitehall a few groans and hisses were heard, but they were speedily drowned by the cheering. Opposite the Home Office some hundreds of well-dressed admirers of the Premier went almost wild with enthusiasm, waving hats and handkerchiefs and cheering voci- ferously. At the point where the roadway narrows into Parliament-street a momentary halt occurred, which was promptly taken advantage of by the crowd. Many persons made a rush at the carriage, and despite the efforts of the police crowded round the vehicle, cheering lustily. Several men managed to seize Mr. Gladstone's hand, which they shook heartily apparently much to the right hon. gentle- man's amusement. Along Parliament-street the windows, doorways, and even housetops were crowded with spectatators.

div.head: HOUSE_ OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE_ OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at a quarter to four o'clock. So great was the crush that chairs had to be placed on the floors of the House for the accommodation of members who were unable to obtain seats, and the ordinary benches and the gal leiies were crowded to an unprecedented extent. The Duke of Cambridge and Prince Christian occnpied seats over the clock. Cheers and counter cheers for the more prominent members was given as they entered. Sir Michael Hicka-Beach was loudly cheered by the Conservatives, and Lord Hartington, who followed soon afterwards, was received with general cheering. Mr. Gladstone entered at 430 and received quite an ovation. The Home Rule members and most of the Liberal members below the gangway rose in their places and cheered again and again. THE ORDERS OF TRH DAY.—Mr. GLADSTONE moved the postponement of the orders of the day until after the mo- tion relating to the Government of Ireland. Mr. Gladstone said it was hoped that the debate on the introduction of the Irish Bill would be finished to•morrow. and if it were pro- longed beyond then the Government would have to con- sider what course to take in regard to the debate, which, however, he trusted might be taken on Monday.
THE FUTURE GOVERNMENT OF IRELAND. MR. GLADSTONE'S STATEMENT.

Mr. GLADSTONE, on rising to submit his motion for the future government of Ireland, was again loudly cheered. He said he could have wished that it had been possible for him to have opened at this moment the whole policy of the Government with regard to Ireland. It was, however, im- possible for him to do so, as the magnitude of the task was too great. What he wished was that they should no longer fence and skirmish with this question, but that they should take measures, if possible, to anticipate the future, and make provision white there was yet time for all the results that might wait on the right or wrong de- cisions of the issue to-day. (Cheers.) We had arrived at a time in the history of Ireland where two roads parted, probably not soon to meet again. The Government thought the time was come when it should endeavour to come to some decision, and it was their intention to propose to the House of Commeus legislation which, if accepted, he be- lieved would liberate Parliament from the restraint under which of late years it had ineffectually struggled to per- form the business of the country, and which would restore good feeling between Ireland and Scotland. (Cheers.) In order to lay the ground for the important measure which the Government asked leave to introduce, it would be neces- sary for him to ask the House to go with him into a brief review of the general features of our course with regard to coercion for repressive criminal legislation in regard to Ireland. The tight hon. gentleman then entered upon the history of the agrarian condition of Ireland during the past 50 years, pointing out that whereas in the earliest part of the period excessive agrarian crime was exceptional, it had under tile repressive laws passed now become habitual .It was not to he denied that there was a great deal of interference with personal liberty in Ireland. Juries would not convict, and the evictions, whether good or bad, were reeisted by the rural population. The consequence of that was to weaken respect for the law. From 1833 to 1885 there were only two years entirely free from the action of special legislation; but the coercion which had been employed had been spurious and ineffectual. Coercion, and if there was to be coercion, which, God forbid, it ought to be adequate to attain its end. The result of it all had been that the law was discredited in Ireland. What was the main reason ? It was because the law came to men with .a foreign aspect. and in a foreign garb. (Loud Home Rule cheers.) He believed that the people of England and Scot- land would never resort to the alternative of the strangest form of coercion until they had tried every other means to govern Ireland. We had not tried every other alternative, be- cause there was one of which experience had been had abroad, namely, stripping the law of its foreign garb and investing it with a domestic character. (Home Rule cheers.) The case of Ireland was not the case of England and Scetland, and the time had come when something was imperatively demanded from us to restore in Ireland the first condi- tions of civil life, and to secure the liberties of the people. (Cheers.) The question was, how to reconcile Imperial unity with diversity of legislation. He instanced the possi- bility of doing this by the cases of Norway and Sweden, and Austria and Hungary, stating that what had been done in these instances was far more than what was required to be done with regard to Ireland. and under far lees favoura- ble circumstances. The Government were not about to pro- pose the repeal of the Act of Union. It was admitted that there should be some reconstruction of the ex- ecutive in Ireland, but how would it be possible. to do it unless we gave Ireland a domestic legislature ? (Home Rule cheers.) What the Government sought was a settlement of the whole question, and they thought they had found that settlement in the establishment by the authority of Parliament of a legisletive body to sit in Dub- lie—(Home Rule cheers)—for the conduct both legislative and administrative—under the conditions which might be prescribed by the Act—of Irish as distinguished from Impe- rial affairs. (Loud Home Rule cheers.) That was the head and front of their offending. In proposing this they ' 'oust see that the unity of the empire was not pieced in danger, and that there should he an equitable distribution of imperial burdens,andnext that in introducing the pro- vision for the peculiar circumstances of Ireland, whose his- tory had been one long chain of internal controversy as ,

well as difficulty, there roust be reasonable safeguards f( r the minority. (Cheers.) This was composed of three clateee, es., they most connider those immediately son- 1 fleeted with the lam] ; secondly, the question offering any , great difficulties relating to the civil eervice ; thirdly, that ' relating to the Protestant minonty. Their duty would be I to adhere to some general principles, and give the utmost I consideration to the opinions of the minority. Ireland was to have a domestic legislature for Irish affairs (Home I Rule cheeis.) That was his position. Then came the gues- I tion, " Are Irish members in this House, and are the Irish representative party in the other House still to continue to form part of the respective assemblies ? " Now, he thought it was perfectly clear that if Ireland was to have a domestic legislature—lrish Peers and Irish representatives could not come hero to control English and Scotch affairs. He be- lieved that wauld be universally admitted. (Home Rule cheers.) One thing followed from the other. His next question was whether it was practicable for Irish representa- tives to come to Westminster for the settlement of Imperial affairs. That opened up the question as to whether it was possible to distinguish between affairs which were Imperial and affairs which were not. He did not believe that mortal man could do so, and therefore it would not be possible for Irish Peers and Irish representatives to come to Westminster for the settlement of Imperial affairs Great Brit would never, he felt sure, force upon Ireland taxation without represen- tation. Thus he did not agree with them in principle. To give up fiscal unity would be to give up the unity of the Empire. He thought that in practice to give up fiscal unity would be great inconvenience and misfortune to both Great Britain and Ireland. He proposed that customs duties, and such excise duties as were immediately connected with them should remain with the Imperial Parliament, but on the condition, first, that the general power of taxation over and above these should pass unequivocally to the domestic legislature of Ireland, and that the en- tire proceeds of Irish customs and excise be held for the benefit of Ireland, for the discharge of the obligations of Ireland, and for the payment of the balances after the dis- charge of those into au Irish Exchequer, to remain at the free disposal of the Irish Legislative Parliament. Irish peers wed members of Parliament would be relieved from attendance at Westminster. For legislative purposes there would be excepted from the sphere of the action of the Irish Parliament everything that related to the Crown—succes- sions, prerogatives, mode of administrative powers during incapacity, ke., all that belonged to defence—the army and navy, the entire organisation of the armed forces—he did not say the police force ; and thirdly, the entire subject of foreign and colonial relations. It would not be competent for the domestic legislature to alter the provisions of the Act which he hoped they were about' to pass—(cheers and ironical cheers)—except on points that were left open. Another desirability would be to provide that the legislative body should not be competent to pass a law for the establishment or endowment of any particular religion. (Home Rule cheers.) With regard to trade and navigation, Ireland would be prohibited from separating herself from Great Britain. The same observation applied to the subjects of coinage and legal tender, but they did not intend to use the word currency. It would be for the convenience both of this country and of Ireland that the Post Office should remain under the control of the Postmaster-General, but the matter would be left open im the bill, so as to enable the domestic legislature to have control of the service, if it thought fit. He now came to the composition of the legislature. He bad referred to the protection of minorities. They might , constitute a legislative body in Irelaisd by a very brief I enactment, simply by saying it should consist of so many members. He proposed to introduce two orders, to sit and deliberate together, with the power in either to demand separate voting, and thus put an absolute veto on a proposal of legislation till the next dissolution, or for a period of three years. Irish members having left the House of Commons, he said Irish representative peers would leave the House of Lords. They would have the optima to sit for life as a I portion of the first order in the Irish legislative assembly. The rest of the first order would consist of 75 members, elected by persons occupying to the value of £25 and up- wards. The second order would consist of representatives of counties, cities, and towns, elected as at present. In the event of any refusal to sit the vacancy should be filled by the machinery now existing. As to Dublin University, it would retain its members as at present, and power would be given to the new legislature ,to appoint a like member for , the Royal Universities. The result would be that the first I order would reach 103 members, and the second order 206 members. With regard to the executive, any changes would work out with time, but respecting the viceroyalty his office would not be altered by statute. The Viceroy, however, would not be the representative of a party, and would not quit office with an outgoing Government. The present religious disabilities attaching to the office would also be removed. (Cheers.) Then as to the judges of the Superior Court. The Government desired to secure to the present judges their position and emoluments exactly as now. As to the future, any judges appointed should hold office during good behaviour, their I salaries to be charged on the Irish Censolidated Fund, and they should be removable only by a joint address from the two orders. Respecting the constabulary, the Government would give a strict assurance to the present members that their conduct should not be prejudiced. The same condi- tion would apply to the Dublin police. The Consolidated Fund of Great Britain should relieve the Irish to the ex- tent of any excess over a million. With respect to the constabulary, literally it would come under the complete control of the legislative body, and as to the civil service, its future members would be absolutely under the control of the domestic legislature, and with regard to the present members, be proposed that the Act should authorise the civil servants now serving to claim the pension due to them, and the abolition of office, provided that they served the period of two years after the passing of the Act. Now as to the equitable distribution of Imperial burden, if we are, to start an Irish legislative body, we must start it with some balance to its credit. (Cheers and counter cheers.) It appeared to him that a fair propor- tion for Ireland to-day would be one-fifteenth of the Imperial expenditure, such charges as the vote of credit not to be included in the total amount. He described the charges for the civil service in Ireland at present, not only as wasteful, but demoralizing. Under present circumstances, the expen- diture of Ireland would be £7,946,000, while her total in- come was £8,350,000, or a certainty of £404,000 to the good. In conclusion, he said there was something more wanted even than the passing of good laws, and that was that they should be passed by the proper persons. They had now to consider whether that was not applicable to Ireland. We stood face to face with Irish nationality. The choice of the Government had been made, and he asked Parliament to aid them in a work which they believed would restore Parliament to its dignity and legislation to its free and un- impeded course, and would secure at once the social peace, the fame, the power, and the permanence of the Empire. The right hon. gentleman resumed his seat amid great cheering, having spoken three hours and twenty-three minutes.

Colonel WARING declared that the Loyalists of Ulster refused to transfer their allegiance from the Queen and from the Imperial Parliament to any other legislative body, and if necessary they would take what steps might be thought advisable to secure their connection with this country.—Mr. MactreoßTEN asserted that the scheme fore. shadowed by the Prime Minister constituted an absolute re- peal of the Union ; while Mr. O'NEILL stated that the Protestant minority were determined to pro- tect themselves by all the means in their power should their liberties or property be assailed.— Sir JAMES PERGUSSON submitted that there could not be a wider separation or a more utter repeal of the legislative Union than that which was proposed.— Mr. SHIRLEY said the electors of the West Riding of York- shire had made up their minds that the Irish people ought to have the fullest measure of local self-government con- sistent with the Unity and integrity of the Empire and the Question now was whether the proposals of Mr. dladetone were consistent with that unity aud integrity.--Mr. TnE- YELVAN explained why he had' left the Government. He did his best to prevent one of the great parties in the State from identifying themselves with what he could but at best regard as neither for the credit nor the welfare of the country. He con- tended that the Nationalist party in Ireland by the laxity of their attitude towards crime had not estab- lished such a title as would justify the House in banding over to them the lives property, and freedom of Irishmen. The other point on which he left the Government was the question of lard. He declined to guarantee half a million to a duke to go away, and leave behind every poor doctor, lawyer, sheriff's officer, and every witness in the old trials. —Mr. PARNELL reminded the House that in the last Par- liament Mr. Trevelyan introduced a bill to buy out the Irish landlords, a scheme which be now denounced. He thanked Mr. Gladstone for his scheme, and he believed that the result would be that the people of England, no less than the people of Ireland, would recognise that the right hon. gentleman in what he had done was a national benefactor. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN moved the adjournment of the debate, and the motion was agre.d to.—Sir W. HARCOURT gave notice that the Prime Minister would move next day to resume the debate then. MISCELLANEOUS.—nr. BRYCE moved the second reading of the International and Colonial Copyright Bill.—After some discussion the second reading was agreed to.—Mr. FRANCIS POWELL introduced a bill to repeal the provisions of the Church Building Acts relating to the compulsory pur- chase of sites for churches and burial grounds. The House adjourned at 12-45.

BARBLsTERS—whose professional labours. necessitate long In- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted natu,e as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. THE QUEEN AND THE COLUMBINE HEROlNE.—Elizabeth Monet, the heroine of the adventure in the smack Colum- bine, has received a letter from the Queen, stating that her Majesty has been much touched by the account of the suffer- ings endured by Miss Mouat, and was pleased to learn that she is recovering her strength. Her Majesty forwards Miss Mouat a cheque for £2O. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Monday, a cab containing George Whittell, farm servant, his wife, and her sister, Mrs. Preston, was standing on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, near Huddersfield, in readi- ness to cross the line after a gate had been opened, when a train came up and dashed into the cab. Mrs. Preston was struck by the engine and died in a few minutes, and the other persons in the vehicle sustained very serious in- juries. .

THE CASE OF MR. LONGSHAI4II_-• At Warriwton County Petty Seetk-ss, Voialike." day, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, solicitor, appeared in suplport of three summonses.taken out with regard to illegal removal of fixtures from a house at Penketh belong- ing to Mr. R. Garnett, and formerly occupied by Mr. Peter Philip Longshaw.—The Magistrates' clerk (Mr. Nicholson) said that Mr. Longshaw, who was formerly in business as a chemical manufacturer at Sankey Bridges, was at present in prison for con- tempt of the Warrington Court.—Mr. Ridgway said that there were three summonses. One was against. Peter Philip Longshaw as a tenant of the house, one against Margaret L. Longshaw as tenant, and another against Peter Philip Longshaw as aiding and abetting Margaret L. Longshaw. The sum- monses were taken out by Mr. Garnett in consequ- ence. of the defendants, or one of them, having removed certain fixtures from the freehold. They had been adjourned from time to time, and now he had to apply to the Bench for permission to with- draw them. The defendants had now had the fix- tures which where the subject of the summonses taken back to Ash Villa, and they were being put in their proper positions. Mr. Garnett did not wish to be vindictive. He had vindicated the law, and would be glad if the Bench would now approve the application.— Mr. A. Browne, who represented Mr. Longshaw, also said that the fixtures were being put back.—The. Bench granted the application, and the summonses were withdrawn. At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. A. Browne applied to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes for the release of the bankrupt from Walton jail. He had filed an affidavit made by the debtor him- self, which was on the file. The second paragraph said that he (the debtor) had made out certain accounts, which, he was informed, and believed, had been filed in that Court, and the affidavit fur- ther said that such accounts had been made out to the best of the bankrupt's ability, and that he had made out all accounts required that his books con- tained; that he had no record of the accounts received from friends and others, and that there- ' fore it was impossible to make out an account of the same; that the remarks made by him on the stock account were correct; and that he had now, been in prison for over two months, during which time he had suffered great privation. Further- more, the bankrupt said that he deeply regretted having brought himself into contempt of the Court, and begged that he might be released from prison, when he would give every assistance in his power to the Court and the Official Receiver to facilitate matters in connection with his estate Mr. Ridgway, Official Receiver, said that he could only refer his Honour to the report already on the file, and leave the matter entirely in his Honour's hands. The accounts were in the same position, and no further ones had been filed. There was no means of checking the papers by the books.—His Honour: Is there no possibility of getting anything better ?—Mr. Ridgway said that he had great doubts on that point. The bankrupt had had the books, and if he had given true information he (Mr. Ridgway) did not know that he could give any further accounts. Bankrupt said he had made the best of it, and he could not say that that was not the. truth.—His Honour said that he did not think that the conduct of the debtor in jail had been such as to ex- cite sympathy. He had no doubt bankrupt's solicitors were aware that bankrupt had presented two petitions to the Secretary of State for the Home Department, which had been referred to his Honour. He said distinctly that those petitions were not correct, and were not couched very pro- perly. The language of the petitions did not show that he was in that penitent position in re- gard to his behaviour before the Court that he now said he was. It might be that lie had come to a better frame of mind, and that the apology he now made was really a sincere and genuine one. After what the Official Receiver had said, and the report that had been rendered, he did not know that it would be any advantage to the creditors to keep the bankrupt in prison, but if he was released now, he must remember that he was still liable to be re- committed if he should not satisfy the Official Re- ceiver in regard to the accounts. If he refused to give assistance to render the accounts more satis- factory, he might be re--committed. With these remarks he would order the release of the bank- rupt.—Mr. Browne said that with regard to the petitions, lie should like to say that he had not the slightest information that they were being sent up. When he heard that they had been sent up he was very much annoyed, and discountenanced the whole affair.—His Honour said that a man was perfectly at liberty to petition, but he was speaking of the language of the petitions.—Mr. Browne: I have never seen the petitions, and have had,nothing to do_z with them.

Mrs. Parnell, mother of the Irish parliamentary leader, still continues very ill. The litest accounts state that the old lady is worse.
A youth named Sanderson, an apprentice to a trainer of racehorses near Marlborough. in Wiltshire, has been sen- tenced to nine months' imprisonment for maliciously injur. ing a horse valued at £5OO.

DRAMATIC RECITAL.—On Friday evening Mr. J. Desvhurst, the well-known tragedian, gave a dramatic recital in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown. There was not a large attendance, but those present fully appreciated the treat that was given them. THE LIVERPOOL RITUAL CASE.—The will of the Judge in the Bell-Cox ritual 'case was read by the Rev. J. A. Lane (acting as surrogate for Lord Penzance), at the sitting of tlAe York Chancery Court, in York Minster, on Thursday morning. The document pointed out an irregularity in the order of suspension, and in ordrT to obviate the possibility of any legal question lying raised, ordered a further sus- pension for six months.

HISSING THE TOAST OF THE QUEEN.—At a public dinner at Stratford-on-Avon, on Saturday, to celebrate the re- turn of Lord William Compton as first member of the divi- sion, when the chairman proposed the toast of the Queen's health there were groans and hisses given by several per. sons. Lord William Compton emphatically protested against such conduct, and said he would never take part in proceedings at which disloyal sentiments were expressed. Eventually the instigator of the disturbance left the room.

DREADFCL TRAGEDY IN MANCHESTER.—At Manchester, on Saturday, a tailoa named Philip Hyman, who has been separated from his wife, went to the house where she lived and a quarrel ensued. He produced a revolver and fired two shots at his 'rife, both taking effect in her head. Thinking he had killed her, he placed the revolver in his mouth and blew his head to pieces. The woman Was seriously injured, and her recovery is doubtful. The man also fired at his daughter, who was attracted by her mother's screams, but the bullet missed.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. FORSTER, M.P.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. FORSTER, M.P.

Mr. W. E. Forster, M P., died on Monday at his residence in London, after a lingering illness. He had another severe attack on Saturday morning, and remained unconscious until about one o'clock on Monday afternoon, when he expired. William Edward Forster was born on Tuly 11th, 1818, at Bradpole, in Dorsetshire. His father, a prominent member of the Society of Friends, distinKiiished himself as an ardent and devoted assailant of slavery, and it WAS while engaged on a mission of emancipation that he met his death in Tennessee. The influence of his parent- age was strongly marked in Ur. Forster's political career. It was not merely that he passionately opposed slavery in every shape or form. Wherever the cause of oppressed Aborigines was to be heard against white tyrants or invaders, Mr. Forster was always ready to uphold it with his utmost force and energy, even at the risk of war. Mr. Forster dis- agreed entirely on these subjects with Ur Bright. and with a large section of the Liberal party, in- cluding on some occasions Mr. Gladstone himself. But he always stood to his guns, and his indomitable firmness earned him general respect. Mr. Forster was expelled from the Society of Friends in conse- quence of what he called the wisest set of his life, his marriage with a lady not a member of the Society, a daughter of Dr. Arnold, of Rugby. He abandoned the theology as well as the peace doctrines of his early associates. He became, if not a member, a strong adherent of the Church of England. Mr. Forster went into business as a worsted manufacturer at Bradford. His first public appearance was made at the age of twenty, when he went to Ireland for the purpose of distributing relief to the victims of the terrible famine which devastated that country in 1846 and 1817. Between 1870 and 1874 he acquired an immense reputation for administrative and Par- liamentary capacity. He conducted both the Educa- tion .A ct and the Ballot Act through the Commons, and the Education Act is usually and properly referred to as his. When Mr. Gladstone returned to office in 1880, 'Mr. Forster entered the Cabinet again, this time as Chief Secretary for Ireland. Is was afterwards known that in Ireland for several months Mr. Forster's life was in great danger. In the spring of 1882, the Government decided to release Mr. Parnell and his fellow-prisoners, on the understanding that they would use their influence in the suppressionl of outrages. Mr. Forster disapproved the step, and resigned. In general politics Mr. Forster continued after his resignation to support the Liberal party. He welcomed the extension of county franchise, and voted steadily with Mr. Gladstone against the post- ponement of the Franchise Bill till after the Redis- tribution Bill had been brought in. But on Egyptian affairs Mr. Forster separated himself from Mr. Glad. stone's Government, advocating a more warlike and aggressive !policy. Mr. Forster also advocated a more decided interference in South African affairs, especi- ally on behalf of the Bechuanas, and here he came into personal collision with Mr. Gladstone, ' who treated him, however, with invariable courtesy. There was scarcely a public question of any importance in which Mr. Forster did not take a prominent part. He was an active worker in the cause of Imperial Federation. Ho stoutly resisted the attempt or the Conservatives to restrict the trade in foreign meat beyond what was necessary for protection against disease. He vehemently opposed the pretensions of the House of Lords to delay the enfranchisement of the people. In the division which turned out Mr. Gladstone's Government in the summer of last year he voted with his eld colleagues. In the latter part of the summer he showed signs of prostration, which ended in death as already stated.

A WARRINGTON PUBLICAN FINED FOR BETTING. At Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, a case of some interest to the betting fraternity was heard before Alderman Harrison (the Mayor), Alderman Davies, and Councillor Greening. John Mather, of the Rose and Crown Thu, Bridge-street, was sum- moned for having on the 25th March, unlawfully used the Rose and Crown for the purpose of betting with persons resorting thereto " upon certain events and contingencies of and relating to certain horse races." The prosecution—the first of the kind insti- tuted in Warrington—was taken at the instance of the police, on whose behalf Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) conducted the case. Defendant was re- I presented by Mr, Brown, solicitor, of Stockport, and Mr. R. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, watched the case on behalf of the owners of the house. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley,. and Co.—Mr. Whittle said that the defendant was charged under section 3 of the Bet- ting Act, 1883, and had made himself liable to a pen.l alty of not more than Lroo and costs, or imprison- ment not exceeding six months. He resided at 81, Bridge st, at the Rose.and Crown, which house he had occupied since 1869. The offence was committed on Friday, the 26th ult., on which day the Grand National was run. A man named Joseph English, who lived at Halewood, met a person at Halewood Station named Mrs Joynson, at ten o'clock on Friday mornine, and as the result of a conversation between them, Mrs Joynson went in the afternoon to the house of the defendant and asked " What are you laying upon 401 d Joe.'" Defendant re- plied " 25 to 1," but on consulting a list, said "No, it is 20 to 1." She said "Put 103 on in the name of Edward Sum. merfield, and 3e for a place for Red Path." She also told him to put 5s on Old Joe in the name of Mrs Summerfield. Old Joe won the race. In consequence of a complaint that defendant would not pay the money whea the race was run, P.C. Neill went to the defendant and said "Is it true that you have been making a bet with a woman named Joyiison. and refused to pay her ? " and his reply was "Yes, lam not going to pay a lot of thieves; the same party has done me about two years ago the same way." Subsequently the same officer served a summons on defendant, who said "What, has it come to that? It is a bad job. I know I shall be fined and I have a big family to keep." Afterwards Inspec- tor James and some constables Aearchecl defendant's house and found the hooks he (Mr. Whittle) had now before him, together with a number of telegrams, some of which bore the date on which the Grand National took place. The police also found a telegraphic code showing the odds upon horses, and a betting book which had been systematically kept. The defendant asked the police if he was bound to turn all the books up, and he was told that he was. The defendant said he had no betting books. He did his bet. I tino• 'on pieces of paper and thee destroyed them. Thel defendant gave a large black book to Inspector James, and while the police were searching, Mrs. Mather reached three telegrams and tore them in the presence of the officers. As the officers were about to leave, the defendant, pointing to a certain book, said "Don't take that book with the elastic baud round it. It is mil John James's. You have no need to take the telegram book, as you cannot read it." He ( Mr. Whittle) contended that there was a clear case of an offence having been committed against the section. He had no desire to press the case, nor had be been instructed to do so. Inotion to back Old Joe. Subsequently she told him the de- fendant had returned the deposit money. He saw Mr. Mather at his house about eight o'clock on Saturday night. He asked him if he had made a bet with Mrs. Joynson, taut defendant said he had had nothing to do with it. The de- fendant would not have anything to do with him, and wit- ness told him it would be better for him to pay the money. The defendamt's wife called hint a thief and a Warrington bully. Several roughs in the bar asked the defendant if he would give them the order to turn witness out, but he did not believe it was Mr. Mather's wish that he should be anused. He gave his money to Mrs. Joynson at ten o'clock on Friday morning. Mary S'umnierfiold, Wife of Edward Summerfield, Sankey Bridges, said that on the day in question her sister, Mrs. Joynson, came to her house at ten minutes to eleven. She left about three in the afternoon to catch the three o'clock 'bus to Warrington. P.O Neill gave evidence bearing out the remarks ot the prosecuting solicitor. For the defence a man named William Cash stated that he was in defendant's house when Mrs. Joynson came in. It would be about ten minutes to four o'clock, and in a few minutes afterwards the result of the Grand National was made known. • Mr. Brown, in addressing the Bench for the defence, said , tbere was no doubt the Celia in this case had been used for , the purpose of revenge, arid the defendant, he maintained; was honourably justified in repudiating the bet. That pro- secution was not brought about in the inter eat of the public, but in the interest of the revengeful spite of title man Eng- lish, who sought to put pressure upon the defendant to pay £lO or £l5. He contended that the house was kept open as a public-house, and not for the purpose of betting, and as there was only one case brought forward it did not go to prove that the house was the habitual resort of betting people. He, therefore, contended that on that ground alone the charge must fail. The Mayor said the magistrates were bound to corns to the conclusion that a bet was made. Mrs. Joynson, it had been proved, did not go to defendant's house to obtain re- freshment, for which the hoase ostensibly existed ; but went there, from something that was told her, to make the bets. At the same time there was a somewhat discreditable element in the case, and that was that the case was not brought for- ward in the interest of public morality,but was instituted, with a spirit of vindictiveness against .Mr. Mather, because he did not pay her the money. The Bencli:would take that matter into their consideration, and would only inflict a fine of £5 and costs, which they thought would meet the justice of the case.

• WARRINGTON RTIIEF COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Warrington Relief Committee was held , in the Mayor's parlour at the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon, when the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) occupied the chair. There were also present the Revs. J. Tinge, E. C. E. Carleton,. and R. Filcher; and Messrs. Greening, T. Litton, F. Monks, S. Davies, .1. timethurst, J. Jolley, and R. Garnett.—Mr. MoNits (secretary) said that 271 c ises had been visited, and 50 had been refused. The number of applications was 325, of which 305 were renewals and only 20 new applications. The number of 4,385 cases had been relieved, which was a reduction from 10,559 the previous week of more than 6,000 cases. The committee recommended that after this week all•able-bodied persons receiving assist- ance from the fund be struck off the list.—The MAYOR tlseught that seemed rather draconic, if it applied to able- bodied persons out of employment.—Mr. GREENING said that the committee would make inquiry, and see if people were in absolute poverty; if so there would be a relaxation of the rule.—The MAYOR: Don't you think it would be as well to put " usless under very exceptional circumstances," because you make an unequivocal resolution not to give relief to any able-bodied people.—The Rev. JOHN YONGE said that agricultural depression was to some extent re- moved, but he did not know whether that applied to other trades.—Mr. MoNKs: To some extent it does.—After a little discussion the following resolution was passed on the motion of the Rev. R. Filcher, seconded by the Rev. John It'onge, viz ,"That power be given to the Executive Committee to strike off the Names of such able-bodied applicants for relief as may be deemed necessarv."—Mr. MONKS remarked that for the six weeks during which the fund had been in exist- ence there had been 48,846 cases relieved, £238 13s 10d had been spent in food and £BO 11s in clothing, total £319 4s 101. —During the meeting it was remarked that the hands at Cockhedge factory were -working full time; that the works of Pearson and Knowles Company and Monks, Hall, and ! Company were working nearly full time, and Mr. GREENING said that at his firm only two or three labourers were out of employ.—The committee adjourned until Tuesday next.

THE UNITERSITY BoAT RACE.—The University Boat Race took plan on Saturday. Cambridge took the lead, but at the Crab Tree Oxford crept up nearly level, and a struggle ensued, Cambridge by a grand effort shooting Hammer- smith Bridge a little in front. At Ceiswick, Oxford again drew ahead, and at Thornevcroft's was over a length in front. At Barnes the Dark Blues increased their adval,tuge, but Cambridee then again gained, and were level at the ship, finishing amid much excitement nearly a length in front. SERIOUS FIRES. On Saturday night, in Tustin-street, Old Kent-road. London, a house, which consisted of eight rooms, caught fire. Mr. Hutchinson, the tenant, had all retreat cut off, when three young men, named Henley, Brooks, and Sullivan, rushed through the flames and car- ried the inmates out in a fainting cendition. The house was completely gutted.—The same night flames were ob- served to be raging in the sunk fiat of the extensive ware- house of Messrs. W. M‘Laren, Sons, and Co., manufac- turers, situated at the corner of Hanover-street and St. George's-square, Glasgow. The warehouse was heavily stocked with Tweed flannels, woollen, and other goods, and before the fire brigade arrived the fire had reached the third storey. Three flats with their contents are a complete mass of debris, but the walls and roof of the build- in are intact. The damage is estimated at from £15,000 to £20,000, which it is believed Is covered by insurance. A large number of hands will probably be temporarily thrown out of employment.— A destructive fire broke out on Sunday morning on the pre- mises of Messrs. Simpson. and Godlee, damask manufac- turers, Dean's Mill, Swinton. The warehouse wee com- pletely gutted, and damage to the extent of about £lO,OOO, which is covered by insurance, caused. About 14 years ago the same warehouse became a prey to the flames. SUPPOSED MURDER IN ENGLAND OF AN AMERICAN GENTLEMAN.—It is believed that the body of Mr. Frederick R. Nours , a wealthy American gentleman, who has been missing for a month past, has been found in the Thames'. Mr. Nourse arrived in London on Fehtuary 21st. Be was in constant correspondence with his wife, whom he left at New York with two children. On the morning of March 3rd he went to Easton Station for the purpose of going to Liverpool, having with him a portmanteau, a handbag, and a hatbox containing a now Lincoln and Bennett. • His port- manteau arrived at Liverpool, but not Mr. Nourse, and from that time down to the present he has not been heard of. His friends offered 100 for his recovery. Posting bills with his photograph were largely distributed. On Tuesday week the body of a gentleman was found floating in the Thames near Battlebridge Stairs and on the follow- ' ing day an inquest was hell. The medical evidence went to show that deceased had first been ill-treated and then thrown into the water. An open verdict was returned. Shortly afterwards Captain Stead telegraphed asking Dr. Fitz Rayne, the surgeon engaged in the case, for further particulars. Dr. Fitzßayne communicated with the cor- oner's officer, and was just in time to prevent the body from being sent off in a parish shell for interment in Woking Cemetery. It is believed that the body may be identified as that of Mr. Nourse by the clothing. The trou- sers pockets were empty, having apparently been ripped down. Dr. Fitzßayne expressed an opinion at the inquest that the body had been in the water about a month, and this corresponds with the time Mr. Nourse has been missing. ESTABLISHED NEARLY 50 YEARS. In' the last Parliament we were accustomed to find under.this heading the personal friends of Mr. Biggar, Mr. Redmond, and Mr. Kenny. This evening order was preserved with greater jealousy, the assemblage being grave and dignified; it really was the ambassadors' gallery. At the other end of the House, above the Press gallery, there was another crowd, unfortunately hid from view, but whose presence was made sensible to the ear. These were the ladies, who, in a fashion even more excit- ing than the Lords, had fcund seats in their cage. The Ladies' gallery is divided into two parts, nearly a third of the space being. devoted to a separate cage which is under the private patronage of the Speaker's wife. Mrs. Peel has had a hard time of it during the last fortnight, Great ladies, accus- tomed to have their wishes instantly gratified, have peremptorily applied for places, to find them all gone. In the other part of the gallery, seats were assigned by ballot, and there was less heart-burning than in the more favoured region where Mrs. 'Glad- stone sat, almost within touch of the Duchess of St. Albans. To such an audience, sections of which had been waiting since six o'clock in the morning, Mr. Glad- stone entered with quick step and somewhat hur- ried look. lis coming was heralded by the faint echo of the cheers of the crowd that thronged the gates of Palace-yard. As usual on these occasions, Mr. Gladstone wore a flower in his coat, one of hundreds that had been sent to Downing-street in the morning by friends known and unknown. On one great occasion in a recent Parliament—l think it was on introducing ope of the land bills—the Premier had ventured td add to the flower a sprig of fern. 'This standing upright, just managed to touch his cheek, and, as he moved his head, exasper- atingly tickled him. The gravity of the occasion was disturbed by the spectacle of the pre-occupied Premier battling with growing desperation with an imaginary fly. To-day he avoided this difficulty by omitting the fern. Usually a little careless in his dress, he was got up with scrupulous' neatness. When the time came for him to speak he had re- gained the composure ruffled by the enthusiastic reception from the crowd outside, but his pale cheek flushed at sound of the prolonged cheering that rose from the Liberal Benches and was echoed from the phalanx of Irish Members massed together on the benches opposite. Of the speech itself, I have not space to write, but is not its purport writ- ten in the chronicles of the day, in all the news paperiof the world? It is understood that the season has not vet commenced. May sees its. opening, June its full bloom, and midway in July comes its sudden de- -cease. No one who is anyone at all—that is to say no one save some three million of people—would be seen in London after Goodwood. There is, never- theless, much of dining and dancing and at-homing going on. No one, for example, carefully picking his way through the brilliant throng at Lady Hayter's last night would guess that the season had not commenced. All the rooms in this beauti- ful house were thrown open, and every one was -crowded., Amongst others present was the Lord Chancellor, lamenting that his duties handicapped him in to-night's race from the Peers to the Com- mons. He must needs remain on the Woolsack till all the formal, business is done, must even walk with solemn steps down the House following the Mace and followed by the purse bearer. By the time he is disrobed it would be easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a Lord Chancellor to get into the Peers'Gallery in the Com- mons. These "At homes" frequently given during the season by certain ladies have considerable effect upon imperial politics. , We have not with recent times had in London anything like the historical salons of Paris. But there are many institutions based upon the saline principle. Mr. Gladstone does not, entertain in a systematic promiscuous manner. He has Thursday morning breakfasts, to which a select few are invited., and occasionally gives a din- ner. Earl Granville is a more general host. Lady Granville's receptions at the Foreign Office were events in the season. Now Lord Rosebery has secured Landsdowne House he shoWs an evident dis- /position to share in the invaluable and indispens- able office of entertainer. Last Thursday Lady Rosebery was "At home," amongst the guests be- ing the Princess Beatrice and Prince Battenberg_ a pretty young gentleman boldly wearing the blue ribbon of the garter in the presence of statesmen, soldiers, and diplomatists, who to win a less royal distinction have done something beyond getting married. For many seasons Lady Hayter has held a, first rank among the London hostesses. The com- pany here is distinctly Liberal, though last night the figure of Mr. Raikes, towering head and shoul- ders high above his fellowmen, moved through the throng and Sir Richard Cross, by exception without the ribbon of the Bath, flitted hither and thither, nnresentful of the many smiles he "heard." There have been rumours for a long time past about the new Gilbert and Sullivan opera. The Mikado has been carrying on with an extraordinary tide of prosperity, but the drop must come sooner or later, and the dramatist must be ready. Mr. Gilbert always rises with the wave. Last year the • wave was Japanese. One saw nothing else, heard of nothing else, talked of nothing else. Now the tide seems to have set in favour of Egypt. When the Academy opens it will be seen how Egyptian subjects have got possession of oil/. artists. The forthcoming Exhibition will give its own help, and by the time the season is over Egypt will have become quite common. Mr. Gilbert will make it more common still. We'll all be reading Antony and Cleopatra, and be surprised to find it is by Shakespere. Mr. Gilbert is determined this time to be even with America in the matter of copy-right. He will get an American citizen to write a very small portion of the dialogue and of the music. In that way New York will only be able to enjoy the new opera on the unaccustomed and disagreeable terms of paying for it. Cheap publications are making us a reading people. Dr. Jekyl has got to -a fifth edition. That perhaps is not to be wondered at, but I hear with astonishment that blue books are largely rising in the market. In the accounts just published it is stated that the price received for blue books has in- creased at the rate of £B,OOO a year. Mr. W. U.

PA.DGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The adjourned debate on Home Rule was resumed on Thursday before a good audience by Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins,- who, 'with the permission of the chairman and the approval of Mr. H. 11. Dutton, who introdueed the subject, substituted for the reso- lution originally submitted to the meeting the fol- lowing :—" That this meeting is of opinion that the people of Ireland should have power to legislate for themselves on all questions which do not affect the imperial interests of the United kingdom. " This was supported by Messrs. Chas. Flinsten, Theodoree. Lon_ don, Frederick Wright, Wm. Broadhurst, and William Bennett, and opposed by Messrs. Ishmael Shaw and Hulse in a long and exceedingly interesting debate. After replies from the gentlemen who had introduced the motion and amendment, which was to the effect that, while the meeting was of opinion that every Irish grievance should be generously dealt with, it was resolutely opposed to the buying out of the Irish landlords and the granting of legislative inde- pendence to that country, a division was taken, in which 15 supported the amendment and 16 opposed it, a considerable number abstaining from voting. The session, which has been exceptionally success- ful, will be brought to a close by a soiree to be held on Thursday next.
