81r,—The Runcorn Union is to be congratulated. At the fortnightly meeting of the Board of Guardians, I hear, the receipt of a communication from the Local Government Board brought forward the subject of the unemployed, and the clerk remarked that there was no increase of pauperism I in the Union, nor were there signs of any unusual amount of distress. A member, commenting on the crowd of pover- ty-stricken labourers attracted by the Ihirlmere water scheme, ventured the opinion that the Ship Canal scheme would bring intl the district an influx of paupers, or words to that effect. A neighbourhood that can despise an increase of labour and consequent increase in the circulation of money that such a vast undertaking would bring about. must indeed be in a flourishing state. The member who made these remarks perhaps forgot that the " paupers " at- tracted would, through the means of labour afforded them, be no longer paupers, but by their industry contribute to the general good —Yours, April 2,1886.
TIMOTHY BODKIN.
A WARNING.

Sir,—My reason for writing is to give a note of warning to your numerous readers respecting a man who is going about the town and representing himself as a German. His "modus operandi" is as follows :•:-.lse calls at your house and inquires if the master can speak German, and if he re- ceives a reply in the negative he asks if Mr. So and So resides at the house, taking care to ascertain by some means that the name be gives is the name of the previous tenant. But the most suspicious part of the affair is when he asked my servant twice to go and ask the master if he could speak German, After her having told him that be (the master) could not do so. It seems pretty clear, to my mind, that if he could have persuaded the servant to leave the door he was intent on: either robbery or mischief. I thought it desirable to send you these few lines as a caution to your readers.—Yours, dec., , Warrington, April 9tb, 1888.
PRUDENCE.
TEMPERANCE REFORII IN WARRINGTON.

Sir,—The other Sunday evening I attended Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel and heard a good sermon by the Rev. J. H. Jones, who spoke in terms meant to pave the way for an ap- proaching gospel mission. By this mission, he said, there was no reason why large numbers of the frequenters of public- houses, and why libertines and harlots, should not be ap- proached and won to the side of religion. This, sir, from an evangelising point of view, is as it should be. I have long been surprised at the apathy shown by our clergy and ministers, and their congregations too, with regard to the welfare of the common people. Each minister seems to go on in a poor, pottering way. lie preaches weekly to his congregation and no doubt does good; but his sphere is too often limited to his well-dressed and respectable parishioners and followers. I have a strong conviction that for drun- kenne.s Warrington can give odds to moat towns of similar siz., but local temperance reformers do not seem to make very especial efforts to meet that state of things. Admitted that they occasionally address a Band of Hope meeting, and urge the benefits of abstinence to audiences composed main- ly of abstainers, but is this enough ? Band of Hope re- unions and old women's tea meetings are right enouah oc- casions to sigh over the degeneracy of fallen man and woman, but are not usually productive of much practical good. In some towns, no larger than this, it is a common thing to see clergymen and ministers of all denominations on the same platform, wearing the "bit of blue," and ad- dressing mixed audiences of a far different class to the usual church and chapel going Communities--alt working in amity for. a common object—but it is not often so in Warrington. No doubt it might be, but no one with influence enough seems to care about it sufficient to take the lead. Useful work might also be done by holding Saturday evening penny readings in various parts of the town and in many other minor ways. It only requires combination and determine- tion.—Yours. tkc., April, MSS.
TEMPERANCE.
FREE PUBLIC LIBRARIES.

Sir,—! am glad to see that some few have at last woke up to the fact that Warrington ought to have a Free Pahlie Library, and if you will allow me I should like to say a few words concerning what I think ought to be one of, if not the most prominent local question. It seems that the people of England decided 30 years since that it was a right and proper thing that they should have books to read at their own homes. Must it be said that Warrington is a generation behind their own countrymen? I am afraid if any person even hinted at such an idea in public, he would not meet with a very favourable reception. Now, mark the consistency ; they reject as absnrd an idea in theory, and yet carry it out to the letter in practice. We can have a torchlight procession and go nearly crazy when the Ship Canal Bill is passed, but a question that in the long run is of more vital importance (since education is at the root of all true prosperity), we can refer to with as much apathy as we should a scheme for supplying blankets to the Hottentots; bat it has been truly said, that on matters concerning his own welfare an English workman can just see about the length of his nese. One objection I have heard raised as an argument against having a Free Library is that it would be of no use, because rif it were free to-morrow there would not be half a dozen working-men who would trouble to take books out; and as an example the paucity of working class visitors to the Museum was given, but I don't think the argument worthy of much consideration; for what is there in the Museum to attract even an educated person •, a large quantity of state seals, fossils, insects, and stuffed birds, and these, with the addition of a small quantity of articles of general interest, constitute the whole of the Warrington Museum. But even supposing that the Warrington working-man at present has not sufficient education to read books, how about the rising generation Are they, too, to be debarred from reading if they choose? If a start is not made of course the workman will never be sufficiently educated. Let the Corporation do their duty, and I think we shall find that the public will be only too pleased to avail them- selves of their just and legal rights.
A SUBSCRIBER.
THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON.

Sir,—The selection of Mr. John Crosfield to centest the representation of this borough is a good one, and will, I hope, be endorsed by the whole body of Liberals in the town. He is a local gentleman, a large employer of labour, and, without doubt, one of the most popular men in War- ringten. Above all, he knows his own mind with regard to political questions. There is no half-hearted, shallow busi- ness about him. On every subject coming before him he will give a definite and straightforward opinion, and that is the sort of thing we want. Now that the heat of the late election has passed away, it is very interesting to look back and recall to mind the tactics displayed on Tory platforms in this town. it more than one meeting, speakers advocated the Fair Trade " ticket, and declared to the working-men that the adoption of that system was the only means of improving trade and raising wages, and immediately afterwards Sir Gilbert rose and informed the audience that he was a Free Trader,. and always had been, but he was favourable to an inquiry irt the matter.

Sir Gilbert Greenell saw the state of the country when food was almost at starvation prices, when the landlords ruled with iron hand, and the poor were like "dumb-driven cattle," when each parson was almighty in his own parish, and the common herd had to kneel at the foot of the local throne. Those were the days of protection. Thank God there is no chance of a return along that dreary road It is all very well to say they don't want to tax food, and that it is only this and that article they seek to protect. But if one particular interest is bolstered up, where are we going to stop, avid where will the line be drawn? Sae the countries which are protected up to the throat better off than we are? I read a week or two ago in " The York Herald "that in one block of builting in that city there were five thousind or more persons in receipt of oat-door relief. On this question of Free Trade Mr. Croefield is sound. He well knows the vast good which has resulted from it. Where are the men who advocated Fair Trade at the last election—the Lowthers, the Ecroyds, and others? Swept off the political scene to make way for men who will uphold the system that has made oar country great. In this active age we want men to represent us who are abreast of the times. There are the great questions of the land and Dinestablishment to be settled, and if Warrington is to have a voice in favour of complete religious, liberty and the freedom of the land, we shall at the first opportunity dispense with the services of a specimen of fossil Toryism, and elect in his stead a man of the people —yours, Ac_,_
FELIX HOLT.
ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH, WARRINGTON:

Sir,—! have waited to see if an abler pen than mine would answer " observer's" letter, and although I know that our worthy Vicar makes it a rule to treat anonymous communications with the contempt they deserve, still I may not be out of place, as a parishioner who has closely watched the prig!), to say a few words. The Vicar, after some years of very hard work in large parishes, of which the fullest testimony is not wanting, did, I believe, accept a beautiful country parish for rest and chancre, but directly he felt better sacriticsd ease and corn- fort, to come out again and be more actively employed in doing all he could for his poorer brethren, and had be not been animated by the best of motives he would never have accepted a parish like St. Barnabas' without a penny. The first night be arrived he was called upon to settle disputes which had been going on, and, although dismayed, he detir- minethto tackle the work and make the best of the position. With what results? The following will show a little of what has been done. Accepting a parish without any stipend, land the four bare walls of an unfinished church, be at once set about needful repairs; next provided books and other ' things for Sunday scholars; then the choir with psalters, dr.c.; began collecting mon..y for bazaars and schools; gat , an endowment for the church; formed a bind; purchased a large supply of books for prizes and parcchial use; organ- ised communicants' classes, sewing classes, mother's meet- ing, dorcas society, an annual charity for poor women, with several other useful matters. The Vicar has also raised, I am told, with the few who have helped the caused, upwards of £1,400 in small sums, for the schools, church, parish, and all things connected. therewith; besides, a kind neighbour

made some additions to the lighting of the church. The !chord managers got up a new harmonium and paid for it in a week, together with several presents from individual ladies. The Vicar has also nearly £l,OOO promised towards a parsonage house ; arel all this under two years. What way we exeect after a fair trial of five years? Respecting the bazaars, it is well known that the first was held at the worst time it could have been, and the second sale of work was got up very hurriedly; but had the subscriptions promised for the fund been placed with the bazaar accounts, instead of being kept separately, a very handsome sum would have bees told off. The churchwardens and their wives have wceked with a woble spirit, and deserve much praise; but let them net be influenced by an "Observer" who does nothing, but con- tinue the struggle till they have helped to place the parish I on a fair footing. A curate, I believe, obtained a title here, bat his first day (Christmas Doe) he wanted to give up, and under a month he pres.uted a doctor's certlficste on the plea of ill health ; but in his case' as in others, our misfortune is that there is no stipend to offer a suitable working man to labour with this mass of people; hence the result. The schools were,only opened .two months before they were filled with scholars, and they are at present over- crowded. Tnere is a large staff of teachers, and the deed provides amply for managers, but again, unfortunately they have nothing to manage with. The school is a speculation, and it is hoped, after et year's trial. they may be able to carry it on. The church choir still maintains its efficiency, and the members, togeeher with our self-denying organist, have shown themselves men to stand by their Vicar and church, without reward or bribe.

In conclusion. I can only say that there are hundreds of poor in this parish loyal Church people, but for want of work, clothes, and other causes, they are unable to give their support or yesence ; but should the tide turn for them, they will not be behind in rallying round a Vicar and his excellent wife, who have done so much for them in, their distress. The Vicar is a friend to the ppor, and proud of his parish ; and let " Observer " come out of his shell, with his friends kit any), and show what they have given or done before trying to damage the poor in the eyes of their Vicar, or him in their eyes. The Vicar has tried to do too much in so short a time, and a few have grown weary of work and begging; but he still sticks to his post to carry on the great work he has undertaken, and I venture to say that he has been excelled by none in the amount he has done in this short time; also, in my bumble opinion (and which I am happy to say is shared by many others who have spoken to me), that few can surpass him in the Church and pulpit. I can only add come and see for yourselves.
PARISHIONER.

PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WIDNES. SALE OF WORK. The annual sale of work in connection with the Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel was commenced on Wed- nesday afternoon. Formerly the proceeds of the sale have been devoted to the reduction of the debt upon the build- ing, now standing at the sum of £7OO. On the present oc- casion, however, the object of the effort was to provide funds for enlarging the structure, which is used in the double capacity as chapel and school. The members con- sist of zealous Christians, who have worked with a con- stancy and heartiness that has ensured success. The con- gregations on Sundays are very frequently inconveniently crowded, and the accommodation provided is far too meagre for the number of children who regularly attend the school. It is probable that next year the Simm's Cross Primitives will by means of a grand bazaar, far surpassing any of their previous ventures, endeavour to liquidate the debt with which they are now burdened, and then with a clear start erect a new and commodious chapel near the present structure. There was a good company present at the opening cere- mony on Wednesday. Mr. J. G. McMinnies, formerly M.P. for Warrington, who had been announced to undertake the chief part in the proceedings, was absent in consequence of illness, and the Rev. J. Calvert officiated in his stead. After devotional exercises, The Rev. J. Calvert said he was very sorry that Mr. Mc- Minnies. who had very kindly consented to open the pro- ceedings, was very ill, and unable to be present. He was sure it wonld be a great disappointment not only to himself but to all present, but they hoped that Mr. McMinnies' life would be spared, and his health vouchsafed to him. If so he had no doubt that Mr. McMinnies would at some future time be very glad to serve the Primitive Methodists of Widnes. (Hear, hear.) The object they had in view that day was to raise funds for the extension of the school pre- mises. The denomination to which they belonged, the Primitive Methodists, was doing a great work in the reli- gious education of the youth of this country. They had 4.104 schools, 405,389 scholars, and 60,092 teachers. There were 27,855 scholars members of the church. (Hear, hear.) At Simm's Cross they had on the conference returns 260 scholars, but he believed they had nearly 280 children on the books. They had 22 teachers, and 50 members in con- nection with the Band of Hope. The recently started Cate- chumian class already numbered 10 members. It was abso- lutely necessary in order to secure success to enlarge the school by an addition of six or eight new class rooms, and their lady friends had been for months stitch, stitcn, stitch- ing, beg, beg, begging, and give, give, giving, too. (Hear, hear.) He paid a compliment to the ladies for the indomi- table spirit, the burning zeal and the self-denial they had displayed in their labours for that chapel and school for years, and they did not intend to relax their efforts until that school was completed, a beautiful chapel erected, and the debt extinguished. He hoped that the debt of the school chapel would speedily be extinguished, so that the church might be a great power for good in that neighbour- hood. He had very much pleasure in pronouncing the sale of work open, and he wished them every success. (Ap- plause.) There were five stalls. Three were laden with plain and fancy needlework of all descriptions, the fourth bad a dis- play of toys and fancy trifles, and the refreshment stall was the fifth. The ladies in charge were Mesdames Owen, Cal- vert, Wiles, Rollason, Adawes, Bradshaw, Williams, Bed- good, Jones, Fox, Hughes, Sage, Webster, Upward, Cross- ley, Mullard, Wharton, and Miss E. H. Wiles. Tables at which a refreshing cup of tea could be obtained were atten- ded to by Miss F. Wiles, Miss Celvert, Miss Crawford, Mrs. Leather, and Mrs. Roome.. Various amusements were provided, including a "Flue art gallery," arr'anged by Mr. V. Griffiths. The Sale of Work was continued on Thursday. In the evening a tea party took place in Malins Temperance Hall, about 150 persons being present. Subsequently a public meeting was held in the Chapel. under the presidency of Dr. McLennan, who was supported by the Revs. J. Calvert, J. Jackson, and W. Wright;. Messrs. S. Owens, L. Drought, T. Bollason, &c.—The Chairman said it gave him the live- liest satisfaction to see in that room so many happy, con- tented, and intelligent people. It was a matter for satisfac- tion and congratulation that their members were increasing so rapidly that it was necessary to enlarge their premises. From a report Mr. Owen had given to him he found that it the Methodist connection during the year 1885 there bad been an increase of 1,187 members, 65 new chapels, 154 mission places, 78 Sunday schools, 968 teachers, and 7,819 'scholars. (Applause.) We wgre all more or less influenced by our surroundings, and each individual in a community should do something either by precept or example to um- prove that which had bad such a powerful influence for good or for evil upon himself or herself. We could enlarge our intellects by reading and digesting the best thoughts of the best men as found in books, and the moral tone of a community could be elevated by social centres such as they bad established in Widnes. (Applause.) Man could not be regarded as aim isolated unit whose character was the result of his own determination. He was to be regarded as the creature of his surroundings. For ill or good every living , soul was an integral part of society, and his Ideterioration was a disorder to the whole body. Now, there existed in Widnes a large number of individuals who live cut oft from educational, social, or moral influences. They lived apart caring for no interests but their own, and certainly had no It-rest in the good name of the town; they were the float- ing population, and it was to this class of beings that Wid- des owed its somewhat notorious popularity. (Hear, hear.) But if all the good done in the, town were slammed up, it would balance a hundred fold the evil that existed in their midst. (Applause.) Knowing, as they did, that evil doers existed in Widnes every man and woman mast do his and her best to extinguish it, and the Primitive M?thodists of Widnes were showing by their work and their increased numbers that they were do- ing everything in their power to lessen the evil in their midst. (Applause,)—The Rev. W. Wright also spoke.—The ltev. J. Jackson, in an address that was intently listened to, said Mr. Gladstone, one of the most highly cultured men in the country, was performing one of the greatest in- tellectual feats ever performed by any man of his age. (Applause.) The question he was discussing was of pro- found interest to the people of this country, and he be- lieved there was a supreme desire in the English mind to year s older reminded than n the b y Mr.eatlilaedpa unznzel an gf eqatuetshtai question d. es evrt taleedin s tHae y church to which they had the honour to belong. Mr. Glad- etone physically would die, but his influence would live for ever—(applaus.-)--and the page of English history would ere long render to him his just tribute of praise.. (Ap- plause.) Their church was unlike Mr. Gladstone physi- cally. He trusted the church wonld renew its youth con- tinually, and that it would, justify its existence. When it ceased to justify its existence he hoped it would die. (Hear, hear.) Their church had seen of vast influence in the moral world, and he earnestly wished it every success. (Appla.ese.)—Tne customary votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. The handsome sum of upwards of LTG was realised by the sale of work.

Tzunutz COURSINCS.—On referee to our advertis- ing columns it will be seen that Mr. James H. Forster, of the Houghton Arms. Earlestown, intends to hold another terrier coursing match this (Saturday) afternoon. TIIS IVED2OO3, AND DISTRICT CRALLENGE CUP.— This football trophy, which was won by the Earlestown club, who defeated Everton F. C. by one goal to none, at the CLOBO of last season's competition, has this week been handed over to the representatives of the Liverpool and District Association. During the period it has been in the possession of the Earlestown Club, it has been kept at the Wellington Ir,n, Earle-street, from which place it was re- moved on Wednesday afternoon. During the present sea- son the Earlestown Club has not had the success of last year, and it will be rememherel that they were thrown out year, this season's competition by the Stanley Club, who attar playing a drawn game of one goal each at Earlestown, de- feated the then cupholders at Liverpool by two pals to none.

div.head: SOCIAL EQUALITY.
div.p: SOCIAL EQUALITY.

Sir,—ln my answer to the letter of Mr. Chapman which began this controversy, I gave, in reply to one of his numerous queries, a definition of what I considered to be Communism. Mr. Chapman apparently accepted that defi- nition as correct, and we have been arguing upon itsince ; but now he says I have got a Communism of my own. I have before pointed out that it is altogether useless to carry on a controversy in which we each attach different meanings to the same term, and consequently it is absolutely neces- sary to let it be known what he considers Communism te be, as he repudiates the only definition that either of us has yet given. But does it not seem strange that Mr. Chapman, the champion of Communism, should have written about half-a-dozen letters without letting us know what it is he is really writing about? lam afraid an impartial observer will be inclined to surmise that he is beginning to feel the ground slipping from beneath him, and that he is therefore anxious to take up a new position, At all events he must Let us have his definition of Communism. Who knows but what it may turn out te be nothing more truculent than Co-operation. If that be the case he and I may quite cor- dially shake hands and declare ourselves to be of the same opinion, though, of course, he will have to admit that the co-operator is a capitalist and likes nothing better than a good return on his investment and a substantial divi." I must confess I was very much interested to lather from his last letter that Mr. Chapman purposes to alter the natural conditions under which we live before be sets up his brand new Communism. It seems to me that this is the way of all visionaries. The man who is going to flv will have nothing to do with the conditions imposed by gravita- tion till be comes flop to the ground with a few broken bones ; the sanguine projector who is ever on the point of discovering the vcret of perpettAl motion gives no heed to the assurance that there is such a physical truth as the conservation of energy till he wastes his fortune or is taken to a mad-home; and it would seem that the Communist has just as little respect for nature's mode of working. •• Nature's plan " is to be completely remodelled in order that conditions may be produced congenial to Communism. I can think of Mr. Chapman earnestly expatiating to a group of incredulous carnivora on the merits of a farina- ceoue diet and on the nutritiens properties of beans and peas, but I cannot think of him as a reconstructor of the universe. This task is altogether too big a one to be under- taken—even for the sake of bringing about conditions fa- vourable to Communism—without a good deal of premedita- tion. _ _

In my first reply to Mr. Chapman, I remarked that he seemed to be thirsting after elementary information. In each succeeding letter the information which he requires appears to become more elementary. In his last letter he rays he "recognises Communism as the outcome of sociology or evolution." This is too bad. "Sociology or evolution," as if the two words were synonymous. It is clear from this and oae or two other passages in his last letter that Mr. Chapman is an evolutionist who knows little about evolution.

_ Mr. Chapman still refuses to see that a capitalist may create his own fortune. To an unprejudiced mind the very fact that a man will voluntarily agree to pay a certain yearly amount for the nse of capital is proof conclusive that that capital enables him to secure additional wealth at least sufficient to repay the claims of the capitalist. If there was no capital that additional wealth would not be created, and therefore surely capital is the creater of it. If Mr. Chapman cannot see this it is due to a defect that I and pro- bably nobody else can remedy, or to mere verbal quib- bling. That little stirpicultaral community of Oneida, which Mr. Chapman brought forward as a prjo(of scientific com- munism, has apparently been abandoned, and now he falls back upon co-operation to furnish an example of what may spring from small beginnings. Well, there are things prac- ticable and things impracticable. The practicable succeed and the impracticab e fail. Co-operation was practicable and in fifty years has risen to its present gigantic propor- tions; Communism, on the other hand, is impracticable, and after a space of two or three thousand years, during which it has been the dream of dreamers, according to Mr. Chapman its most promising outcome is a colony of three r hundred persons all told in the state of New York. In conclusion, I would again urge upon Mr. Chapman the necessity of letting us know what he considers Communism ,to be. He has repudiated the definition upon which we have been arguing all along, and it is of course necessary that we should know what he is really contending for. , Judging from passages in his last letter. Communistn, in his opinion, may be synonymous with Bud hism. Christanity, ? and Mabomedanism,'' or the " great Republic of , America." JAQUES.

div.head: NOW, AND THEN.
div.p: NOW, AND THEN.

Sir,—l hope my friend Mr. Carleton will keep his mind easy respecting myself. Ido not intend that either he, or his clerical brethrenrshall be allowed to make things com- fortable for themselves, and at the expense of the commu- nity. I can assure him that the vast majority of the people are boginniag to look at the clergy, and the Establishment they so disinterestedly support, with anything but satisfac- tion. They cannot close their eyes to the fact that there is neither a movement nor an institution whose primary object may be the benefiting of the working classes, but what the Church, through its dignitaries, opposes with all its power. I wish to be fair, and I now say that the clergy are forced into evil courses, not through any fault of their own but in consequence of the stilted and barbaric teachings of their Church. Ere I close this letter I hope to make this clear.

With the Church, as an establishment so completely or- ganised, and penetrating as it does into the homes of all classes, rich and poor alike, we have a right to expect more from it than what we have as yet received. I contend that the " Happy England," qualify the expression as you may, we have to-day, we have in spite of the Church, and not because of any of her favours. What does the history of Nonconformity give to us but a long wearisome tale of per- secutions on the part of the Church. The Bishop of Pete.- borough, in moving the second reading of his Parish Churches Bill, has nothing but contumely to heap upon his Nonconformist fellow Christians, and yet none can deny but what the first man who refused to conform, by that very act opened out the way for intellect to assert itself.

In looking through the Thint3 of 31arch 20th, 1 find noble Lords.with a legal acquaiatance of the criminal classes, not to be questioned, battling all alone for the opening of museums on ?handays. Seven bishops were present when Lord Thin.- low brought forward his measure, and yet not one of them spoke for or against it. Mark now; they all voted against tne meahure, and why As Lord Bramwell said. "It was the religious part of the question that was at the bottom of the opposition." Then how was it that the Bishops did net attend, and IT voice and act oppose the measure I answer policy tied seven tongues, and policy kept away the remainder. Had it been a question in convocation, as to facing east, or wearing a gown, how the walls would have resounded ; being a question of making) it possible for a workingman to pass a few happy hours en a rest day, they withheld their support. and yet these same men know, as well as I know, that a large proportion of the wealthier classes pass their Sunday afternoons with cards and bil- liards.

I often wonder how it is that the clergy are. so unani- mous in their Toryism. I take it that the traditions of the Tory party are supposed to teach us to adhere to an- cient usages. If this be so, let us hare bull baitings, bear baitngs, cock fightings, with Burnblculon going round the town staff in hand, and threatenings on the tongue, driving all to church.

Trinity Church. famous to-day in having the Bev. E. C. E. Carleton as pastor,was once famous in having a "bobber," Betty Finch by name. "She walked majestically along the aisles during the service, armed with a long stick like a fishing rod, which had a bob.' fastened to the end of it, and when she caught anyone sleeping or talking she gave him a nudge. Her son was engaged in the belfry, and often truthfully sung—
"My father's a clerk, My sister's a sinzer, My mother's the bobber, And I am a ringer." •

In these good old days the Church looked well after the people. Nonconformity, Agnosticism, Atheism, in fact int-fleet, in whatever shape it came, was told off A SmithUeld that brooked no argument. And what came of it? In " Warrington in the Thirteenth Century " occurs the following :—" Hanging up in the Warrington Museum may be seen a representation of a withered female face wearing the brank or scold's bridle; one of which instru- ments, as inflexible as iron and ingenuity can make it, for keeping an unruly tongue quiet by mechanical means, hangs up beside it. Almost within the time of living ' memory, Cicily Pewsill, an inmate of the workhouse, and a notorious scold, was seen wearing this disagreeable head- gear in the streets of Warrington for half an hour or I more."

In those good old times the Church believed force was a remedy, only it must be the force emanating from its own infallible self. Thus we see society in the past linked with the Church by chains forged in barbarism.

The church. clergy, as a body, claim privileges that, were they accorded, would debase the people; proof for this state- ment abounds in the Book of Common Prayer. Speaking of disestablishment, a church dignitary said recently, "If the measure be curled, which God forbid, this nation must cease to be great." From this it would appear that the industrial resources of the country count for little, and yet how are the religious societies supported in answer to appeals from the platform of Exeter Hall P From the re- port of one of these societies, I find it stated that a nunAer of their committeemen, who are well-to-do people in the City, think that they have discharged their own duty when they have subscribed a five pound note each, which, after all, is not quite tete) shillings a week. Their,anxiety did not rise as high as half-a-crown. One reverend gentleman, whose income is nearer two thousand than one thousand a year, figures for a guinea, which amounts to the rmagnificent sum of fourpence three-farthings a week. A prosperous city solicitor subscribes the same amount. A manufacturerengaged in a very profitable business, employing hundreds of harms, ' subscribes two shillings a week. A city merchant, who rides in his carriage and lives in a stately mansion, is equally munificent. Another, who is a member of an eminent firm, is centent with the regulation guinea, or fourpence three- farthings a week. A wealthy corn merchant gives ninepence a week. Another noble-hearted man of business, who makes over twenty thousand pounds a year, gives the regulation guinea, or fourpence three-farthings a week. We could multiply such examples almost ad libitum."
CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
_ In South Somerset, on Friday morning, there was a heavy snowfall preceded by hailstorm. In 'Yeah Wales there also was a snowstorm.

M. Vandersmissen, a lawyer and deputy for Brussels, on Thursday night fired six shets from a revolver at his wife, mortally wounding he-. TRIAL OF SOCIALISTS. Messrs. Ilyndman, Burns. Williams, and Champion, the London Socialists, were again charged at Old Bailey, on Friday, with uttering seditious language. The whole hearing was occupied with defence. —The Hon. Howard Spensley, M.P., said he thought . Champion an earnest man, and that he desired to benefit the ! working-classes.—Mr. Burleigh, special correspondent of the "Daily Telegraph," denied that Burns made use of the expression about bread and lead.—A man called Spading deposed that he made use of the term.—Mr. Thompson and Mr. Burns then addressed the jury, and the case was ad- journed. FUNERAL SERVICE OF THE LATE MR. FORSTER.—The funeral.servica of the lat , Mr. Forster took place at noon, on Friday, in Westminster Abbey. The Dean conducted the service, which was of a very impressive character. The coffin was covered with blue cloth, and bore the simple in- scription " William Edward Forster, died April 6th. 1886, aged 67." It was literally covered with floral wreaths sent from Ireland and all parts of the country. There was a large attendance, including members of both Houses of Par- liament. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone were present, as were also Lords Granville, Rosebery, Selborne, Ripon, Coleridge, Iddesleigh, Cowper, De Vesci, Fitzgerald, Wolcieley, Messrs. Alfred Illingworth and Angus Holden Mr. Forster's col- leagues in the representation of Bradford. The service was fully choral. The body was afterwards removed for inter- ment at Burley-in-Wharfedale.
THE POLITICAL SITUATION. RESIGNATION OF MR. HE-NEAGE.

The Central News Understands that Mr. Heneage, Chan- cellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, has, in consequence of the nature of Mr. Gladstone's declaration, placed his resig- nation in the Premier's hands. CABINET COUNCIL.

A Cabinet Council was held at Downing-street at two o'clock, all the members being present. It is understood that the Irish measures were but briefly referred to, the chief object of the council being to arrange the order of business in the House ot Commons.

div.head: MEETINti OF CONSERVATIVE LEADERS.
div.p: MEETINti OF CONSERVATIVE LEADERS.

A meeting of the ConseryetiAe leadeis, convened by the Marquis of Salisbury, was held at Arlington-street, at noon on Friday. There were present the Marquis of Salisbury, the Duke of Richmond, Lord Iddesleigh (who arrived late from attending Mr. Furster's funeral service at Westminster Abbey), Lord Harrowby, Lord John Manners, Lord R. Churchill. Lord Cranbrook, Lord Salisbury, Lord George Hamilton, Sir M. Hicks-Beech, Sir R. Cross,. Mr. Stanhope, Mr. W. H. Smith, Colonel Stanley, and Lard Ashbourne. The senior Conservative whip, Mr. Akers Douglas, was in attendance. The proceedings at Arlington-street were almost confined to a conversational discussion respecting Mr. Glad- stone's Irish Government scheme. Opinion was found to be unanimously and emphatically in favour of offering the Government proposals a strenuous and persistent opposition. The Conservative leaders separated at ten minutes pas one, with the unders,anding that a general meeting of the party shall be held next week.

div.head: SUPPRESSION OF SOCIALIST NEWSPAPERS.
div.p: SUPPRESSION OF SOCIALIST NEWSPAPERS.
BRUSSELS, FRIDAY Af TERNOON.—The police have seized two Socialist newspapers here and closed the printing offices.
REPORTED CHOLERA OUTBREAK IN FRANCE.
PARIS. FRlDAY.—Respecting the cholera in Brittany, the Phare de a Loire to-day says the sanitary condition of Treboul is improvedtenly fourteen cases being under treat- ment.

div.head: MURDEROUS ATTACK ON A FRENCH SUB-PREFECT.
div.p: MURDEROUS ATTACK ON A FRENCH SUB-PREFECT.

PARIS, 1‘ RlDAY.—rae Sub-Prefect of Latour du Pin in the department of Isere, having gone to La Combe to close a chapel situated en some private land, was, assailed on his. arrival by the inhabitants with pistol shota and stones. The Sub-Prefect and three gendarmes were wounded, and one woman was killed.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock.

TRIBUTB TO Ma. FORSTER--The Contagious Diseases Acts Repeal Bill was read a second time.—On the second reading of the Poor Relief (Ireland) Bill Earl SPENCER pain a high tribute to Mr. Forster, with whom he was associated the last time a bill of that kind passed through the House. Mr. Forster was remarkable for his honesty,. great love of liberty, and his life-long effort to remedy abuses.—Lord IDDESLEIGH had never known a man more thoroughly hon- ourable, more thoroughly trustworthy, or who showed more courage in dealing with grave dangers.—Lord Cows con- curred, and the bill was read a second time, and the. House adjourned. The House met at four o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

There was a very fall attendance when the Speaker took the chair. The Duke of Connaught and the Duke of Cam- bridge occupied seats in the Peers' Gallery, which. like other parts of tke House, was fully occupied. Mr. Cham- berlain took a seat on the end of the second bench below the gangway on the Ministerial side of the House. . _

QUESTIONS, &C.--Mr. THEODORE FRY gave notice that on an early day he should move a resolution to extend the hours of polling at School Board elections.—Mr. MON- DELLA, replying to 11,1 r. Addison, said the Government had no power to interfere with regard to the employment of foreign seamen in the mercantile marine —Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Mr. Abrahams said he had no power to airect that all persons appointed to Welsh County Courts judge- ships should understand the Welsh language. ORDER OP BUSINESS.-Mr. GLADSTONE intimated that if the debate on the Government of Ireland Bill was not con- cluded it would be continued on Monday. The financial statement therefore would be made on Tuesday ; the ad- journment for Easter wduld be from Monday before Good Friday to the Monday following Easter Monday. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF IRELAND BILL.

Mr. CHAMBERLMN, rising to resume the debate, was re- ceived with slight cheering. He asked the indulgence of the House while he-explained the circumstances that led to his resigning his position in the Government, Since he and Mr. Trevelyan had left the Government, rumour had been busy and not always with truth. He denied that he had entered the Government with the desire to wreck it, and said no act in his public life had been so painful as his separation from oae he had so long followed and honoured; but the question of the integrity of the empire was so vital, and mistake, if made, so fatal and irrevocable that it was but right to bring private judgment to bear on the subject; and it was because he believed the integrity of the empire was in danger that he made tbe greatest sacrifice any poli- tical man conk', make. He then related the circumstances of entering the Government, and said he lathed it because he believed the declarations made to him on entering it were not fulfilled in the scheme ef the Primo•Minister for the Government of Ireland. He was not opposed to Home Rule, as he understood the term. He was prepared to give the largest measure of local government possible with dos regard to the integrity of the empire and the control of Parliament, and it was because he believed this plan did not fulfil that condition that he left the Gorernment. Re was then about to enter into certain explanations as to the Land Purchase Scheme, when Mr. Greensavern intimated that he was going beyond the limits accorded by her Majesty, to which Mr. CinveinErtmeeter exciaimed—" How am I to explain with my hands tied behind me !" which elicited great cheering. He then proceeded to give his ob- jections to the plan of the Government, the first being the exclusion of Irish members from that House, be- cause he felt if they were net in that House the Irish Parliament would be eqoal to the Eng- lish. He further objected to the plan because it renounced all taxation, placed the appointment of the • judges and magistrates in the new legislation, and because the proposition made the new legielature supreme in all matters not excluded by the bill. One important alterative, had been made siece he left the cabinet, and that was that the customs and excise were to be collected by impeeial authority, but that did not go far enough, as they had not the lrieh members in the English Parliament, wh reit he thought a degradation. ("No no,' from liith members.) Well, he contended, the Irish members were the best judges of that. Having asked for further explanations as to the scheme regarding trade and navigation, he summarised his objection not to any poation of the plan by saving he objected to it as a whole. He strongly objected to the financial proposals because he believed it was exposing British taxpayers to excessive risk, and he was not inclined to do that in order to pass a thinly veiled scheme of separation. Whatever might be the course taken by Irishmen in that House, be felt sure the country would never accept it. Rather than fate the irritation the planewould excite, rather than face the distraction in all domestic legislation the plan would create, he would vote for separation pure and simple. (Loud cheering.) He would wipe off all Ireland's liabili- ties as a bad debt, and let him or her go free, as, he said, I he was certain the plan would come to that in the end. He I expressed the opinion that the true solution, he firmly be- lieved, was to be found in some sort of federation that

would preserve the unity of the empire. He then again jurtitied the course he had taken, and said he should feel increditable shame had he supported a policy be thought in his heart was injurious to the best inter- ests both of Ireland and of theat Britain. (Cheers.)--- Mr. HEALY severely criticised the speech of Mr. Cham- berlain. He pointed out the great stand he had made abo!it protection to the loyal population of Ireland, and yet in all Mr. Chamberlain's sentences about councils be bad not said a single word about their protection. He presumed that was to be accounted for by the f..ct that he had not- thought out his scheme enough. He believed when *the plan of the Prime Minister became fuliy known it would be accepted with welcome by the Protestants, because it would be felt it was a noble attempt to do right to Ireland. He and those around him would give the Prima Minister their best support in order to enable him to carry his noble attempt to a successful issue, and thus do their best to , unite for ever the two nations in the bond of amity and peace.

Mr. W. Ara.mg thought the present proposal of the Government was so momentous that the constituencies of the three kingdoms ought to be consulted. He candidly ad' mitted that the speech of the Prime Minister, whom he bad followed for 20 years, appeared to him to be a bribe the Irish members. He sincerely helieved that giving a separate Parliament for Ireland would in the end result io the total separation of Ireland from the British Crown. ‘_ W. JOHNSTONE described the bill as one not so loung for establishing separate legislature for Ireland as for legalizing the councils of the National League. [LEFr SITTING.]

The outgo. was £376 los, leaving a balance of 12s 3d due to the surveyor.—Mr. Wm. Owen proposed, and Mr. Peter .1 Johnson seconded the adoption of the accounts. -- Mr. John Heaton proposed that Mr. John Ilowortiv be re-elected surveyor. This was seconded by M. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARD.INGTON. —For week endino. Saturday, April 31,(1, 1886.—The mean temperature was 45.8 Fahr., and therefore 5.3 deg. colder than the preceding week. The maxi- mum e'temperature 61 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 3rd ink., and the minimum temperature. 36 Fahrenheit, on the Ist inst. The rainfall measured .57in. The general direction of the wind was W. During the week, which was the 14th of the current year, 35 births and 17 deaths- were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 1907. per 1,000, against 25.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 274 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from diarrhcea, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from enteric fever, 1 from tubercular disease, 1 from heart disease, 3 from brain disease, 4 from lung disease, and 1 from amputation of leg. Three cases of whoop ing cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.
